lessons.content:
THE CTS-D CERTIFICATION

The CTS-D is AVIXA's specialty certification for professionals who design audiovisual systems. While the CTS credential validates operational AV knowledge, the CTS-D focuses specifically on the design process — from initial client consultation through documentation delivery.

EXAM STRUCTURE

The exam contains 110 scored multiple-choice and scenario-based questions, with additional unscored pilot questions bringing the total to approximately 135. You have 150 minutes (2.5 hours). The passing score is 350 out of 500. A math formula reference sheet is provided on screen — you do NOT need to memorize formulas, but you must know when and how to apply them.

DOMAIN WEIGHTINGS — YOUR STUDY ROADMAP

Duty C (Develop and Document AV Designs) is the largest at 38% — roughly 42 questions. This is where display sizing, signal flow, equipment selection, and documentation live. Duty B (Coordinate with Other Professionals) at 28% covers working with architects, MEP engineers, IT, acousticians, and other trades. Duty A (Conduct Needs Assessment) at 20% tests your ability to gather requirements and create program reports. Duty D (Deploy AV Designs) at 14% covers installation support, commissioning, and closeout.

THE DESIGN MINDSET SHIFT

CTS questions ask 'what is this?' — CTS-D questions ask 'what should you do and why?' You'll encounter scenario-based questions where you must choose the best design decision given constraints. The exam tests your ability to think through trade-offs: cost vs. performance, aesthetic requirements vs. technical needs, client expectations vs. physical limitations.

KEY EXAM STRATEGIES

1. Answer every question — there is no penalty for guessing
2. Flag and return — don't spend more than 90 seconds on any question
3. Read the scenario carefully — the answer is often in the constraints described
4. When two answers seem correct, choose the one that addresses the design intent, not just the technical specification
5. Math questions: set up the formula first, then calculate. The formula sheet is your friend.

scenarios.situation: A colleague asks whether they should take CTS-D before gaining significant design experience.
scenarios.notice: CTS-D requires a valid CTS plus 2+ years of AV design experience. AVIXA recommends 3-4 years.
scenarios.nextStep: Advise them to build hands-on design experience first, as the exam tests practical design judgment, not just knowledge.
scenarios.whyMatters: The CTS-D is scenario-heavy. Without real design experience, candidates struggle with the contextual decision-making questions that dominate the exam.

lessons.examRelevance: Understanding the exam structure itself is worth 0 direct points, but strategic preparation based on domain weightings dramatically improves your score. Spend proportional study time: 38% on Design/Documentation, 28% on Coordination, 20% on Needs Assessment, 14% on Deployment.

lessons.title: Needs Assessment: Stakeholders & Functional Requirements
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.domainAlignment: Duty A — Conduct a Needs Assessment (20%)
lessons.overview: Master the needs assessment process: identifying stakeholders, gathering functional requirements, conducting site surveys, and translating user needs into AV system specifications. This is the foundation of every successful AV design.
learningObjectives: Identify all stakeholder types in an AV project and their roles in the decision-making process
Distinguish between functional requirements and technical specifications
Conduct an effective site survey covering environmental, structural, and infrastructure factors
Translate client language into AV system requirements
Create user stories that drive AV design decisions

keyTerms.definition: Descriptions of what the AV system must do from the user's perspective, without specifying technology choices.
Any person or group with an interest in the AV project outcome — including end users, facility managers, IT departments, and executive sponsors.
Physical inspection of the project location to document environmental conditions, existing infrastructure, and constraints affecting AV design.
A statement describing a user's need: 'As a [role], I need to [action] so that [benefit].' Used to drive design requirements.

lessons.content:
THE NEEDS ASSESSMENT PROCESS

Every AV design begins with understanding what the client actually needs — not what equipment they think they want. The needs assessment is Duty A on the CTS-D exam (20%) and the foundation that every subsequent design decision builds upon.

IDENTIFYING STAKEHOLDERS

Stakeholders fall into several categories:
- Decision makers: executives, facilities directors, IT leadership — they approve scope and budget
- End users: presenters, meeting participants, operators — they use the system daily
- Technical stakeholders: IT administrators, facilities maintenance — they support and maintain the system
- Allied professionals: architects, MEP engineers, acousticians — they impact the physical environment
- External stakeholders: ADA compliance officers, fire marshals, building inspectors

Critical CTS-D concept: The person requesting the system is often NOT the primary user. Design for the actual end users, not just the person signing the purchase order.

GATHERING FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

Functional requirements describe WHAT the system must do, not HOW:
- 'Participants in the rear of the room must clearly read spreadsheet data on screen' (functional)
- 'Install a 98-inch 4K display' (technical specification — not a functional requirement)

Key requirement categories:
1. Communication needs: Who needs to communicate with whom? In what direction? (one-to-many, many-to-many, remote participation)
2. Content types: What will be displayed/heard? (presentations, video conferencing, digital signage, live events)
3. User experience expectations: What skill level are the operators? Is a single-button start required?
4. Accessibility: ADA requirements, hearing assistance, visual accommodations
5. Scalability: Future growth, technology refresh cycles

SITE SURVEY ESSENTIALS

The site survey documents everything that affects design:
- Room dimensions (length, width, ceiling height)
- Ambient light levels (windows, artificial lighting, light control options)
- Ambient noise levels (HVAC, adjacent spaces, exterior)
- Existing infrastructure (conduit paths, power availability, network drops)
- Structural elements (ceiling type, wall construction, floor composition)
- Furniture layout and seating arrangements
- Sight lines and viewing angles
- Access for installation (doorways, elevators, loading docks)

TRANSLATING CLIENT LANGUAGE

Clients say: 'We want a video wall.' A CTS-D designer asks: 'What content will be displayed? At what viewing distance? How many simultaneous sources? What's the ambient light environment?' Then translates the functional need into the appropriate technical solution — which might be a video wall, a large-format display, or a projection system.

scenarios.situation: A client says 'We need a projector in our boardroom' during the initial meeting.
scenarios.notice: The client is specifying a solution, not a requirement. They may not know alternatives exist.
scenarios.nextStep: Ask about the actual need: 'What will people in the room need to see? How many will be in the room? Are the lights typically on or off?' Then determine whether projection, a flat panel display, or an LED wall best serves the functional requirement.
scenarios.whyMatters: CTS-D designers solve for needs, not requests. A 'projector' request in a high-ambient-light room with 8 participants might be best served by a 75-inch display.

scenarios.situation: The IT director demands all AV equipment use the corporate VLAN, but the AV system requires multicast traffic for video distribution.
scenarios.notice: Network requirements conflict between IT security policy and AV functionality.
scenarios.nextStep: Document the multicast requirement as a functional need and schedule a coordination meeting with IT to discuss a dedicated AV VLAN with appropriate QoS policies.
scenarios.whyMatters: Identifying cross-disciplinary conflicts during needs assessment prevents costly redesigns during installation.

lessons.examRelevance: Duty A accounts for 20% of the CTS-D exam. Questions focus on: identifying the RIGHT stakeholders, distinguishing functional requirements from technical specs, conducting thorough site surveys, and creating program reports. Expect scenario questions where you must determine the correct next step in the needs assessment process.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which statement is a functional requirement?

Remote participants must hear in-room speech clearly with minimal echo
Use a Crestron DM-NVX system for video distribution
Run Cat6A cables to all display locations
knowledgeCheck.answer: Remote participants must hear in-room speech clearly with minimal echo
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Functional requirements describe what the system must achieve from the user's perspective, not specific equipment or technology choices.

knowledgeCheck.question: During a site survey, you notice the ceiling is an open plenum with exposed ductwork at 14 feet. What must you document?
options: Ceiling height, type (open plenum), structural attachment points, and plenum-rated cable requirements
Nothing — ceiling details are the architect's responsibility
knowledgeCheck.answer: Ceiling height, type (open plenum), structural attachment points, and plenum-rated cable requirements
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Open plenum ceilings affect speaker mounting, cable routing (must use plenum-rated), projector mounting, and microphone placement. All factors must be documented.

memorize: Five stakeholder categories: decision makers, end users, technical, allied professionals, external
Site survey checklist: dimensions, light, noise, infrastructure, structural, furniture, sight lines, access
understand: The difference between functional requirements and technical specifications
Why designing for the actual end user matters more than satisfying the purchaser
practice: Write functional requirements for a 20-person conference room from scratch
Conduct a mock site survey of any room — document everything that would affect AV design
examTraps: A 'requirement' that names a specific product is a specification, not a functional requirement
Don't assume the client knows what they need — the CTS-D designer's job is to uncover true requirements
studyNotes.fieldTip: Always photograph the site survey. Document ceiling grid patterns, outlet locations, and structural anomalies. Photos save revisits.

lessons.summary: Needs assessment is the foundation of CTS-D design work. Identify all stakeholders, gather functional requirements (not product requests), conduct thorough site surveys, and document everything in a program report. The key CTS-D skill is translating 'we want a projector' into the functional need it represents, then designing the optimal solution.

lessons.title: Technology Master Plans & Program Reports
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.overview: Learn to create and review technology master plans that guide multi-phase AV implementations, and generate comprehensive program reports that document all needs assessment findings for design teams.
learningObjectives: Define the purpose and components of a technology master plan
Create a program report that captures functional requirements, site conditions, and design constraints
Understand how master plans align with organizational technology refresh cycles
Document room typologies and standardization strategies
Establish design standards that ensure consistency across an enterprise deployment

keyTerms.definition: A strategic document defining an organization's AV technology roadmap, including standards, room types, deployment phases, and lifecycle management.
A classification system for space types (huddle room, medium conference, large boardroom, training room, etc.) with standardized AV packages for each.
The complete cost of an AV system including equipment, installation, programming, training, maintenance, and eventual replacement.
The planned interval for replacing or upgrading AV technology, typically 5-7 years for enterprise systems.
A specification guide defining approved equipment, wiring standards, naming conventions, and configuration templates for consistent deployment.

lessons.content:
TECHNOLOGY MASTER PLANS

A technology master plan is a strategic document that guides AV implementation across an organization. Unlike a single-room design, it establishes the framework for consistent, scalable AV deployment across dozens or hundreds of spaces.

MASTER PLAN COMPONENTS

1. Current State Assessment: Inventory of existing AV systems, their condition, and capabilities
2. Future State Vision: Where the organization wants to be technologically in 3-5 years
3. Room Typologies: Standardized categories with defined AV packages
4. Infrastructure Standards: Cable types, pathway requirements, power specifications
5. Equipment Standards: Approved manufacturers and models for each component category
6. Deployment Phases: Prioritized rollout schedule aligned with budget cycles
7. Lifecycle Management: Technology refresh cycles and maintenance budgets
8. Budget Framework: Capital expenditure projections by phase

ROOM TYPOLOGIES — THE CORE OF ENTERPRISE AV

Standard typologies for corporate environments:
- Type A: Huddle Room (2-4 people) — display, camera, USB conferencing
- Type B: Small Conference (6-8 people) — display, ceiling mics, DSP, camera, wireless sharing
- Type C: Medium Conference (10-16 people) — dual displays, ceiling mic array, DSP, PTZ camera, control panel
- Type D: Large Boardroom (16-30 people) — video wall or large display, distributed speakers, multiple ceiling mics, tracking camera, full control system
- Type E: Training Room (20-40 people) — projection, distributed audio, recording capability, breakout support
- Type F: All-Hands / Town Hall (50+) — professional-grade PA, multiple displays/projection, production switching, streaming

PROGRAM REPORTS

The program report is the deliverable from the needs assessment phase. It serves as the 'contract' between client expectations and design intent.

Program Report Contents:
- Executive summary of project scope
- Stakeholder interview findings
- Functional requirements (prioritized as must-have, should-have, nice-to-have)
- Site survey documentation with photos and measurements
- Environmental conditions (ambient light, noise, HVAC)
- Existing infrastructure assessment
- ADA and code compliance requirements
- Preliminary budget range
- Project timeline and phase breakdown
- Risk assessment and mitigation strategies
- Approval signatures

DESIGN STANDARDS FOR CONSISTENCY

Enterprise AV benefits from standardization:
- Reduces training requirements (operators learn one system)
- Simplifies maintenance and spare parts inventory
- Enables remote monitoring and management at scale
- Reduces design time for new spaces
- Provides predictable budgeting

The CTS-D designer must balance standardization with the unique requirements of individual spaces. A boardroom used for investor presentations has different needs than a standard conference room, even if both are 'Type D' in the master plan.

scenarios.situation: A university client wants to upgrade 200 classrooms over 3 years but has no existing AV standards.
scenarios.notice: Without a master plan, 200 individual designs would be inconsistent, over-budget, and impossible to maintain.
scenarios.nextStep: Propose a technology master plan engagement before starting design work. Define 3-4 classroom typologies, establish equipment and infrastructure standards, then apply them consistently.
scenarios.whyMatters: The CTS-D exam tests understanding of master planning as a prerequisite for large-scale deployments. Jumping straight to design without a plan is a red-flag answer.

lessons.examRelevance: Tasks A2 (Technology Master Plan) and A3 (Program Report) together represent 13% of the exam. Expect questions about what belongs in a master plan vs. a program report, when to recommend a master plan engagement, and how room typologies drive standardized design.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of a technology master plan?
options: To specify exact equipment for each room
To provide a strategic framework for consistent, phased AV deployment
To replace the need for individual room designs
To document existing AV equipment inventory only
knowledgeCheck.answer: To provide a strategic framework for consistent, phased AV deployment
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A master plan guides the overall approach — individual room designs still happen, but within the framework the master plan establishes.

knowledgeCheck.question: A program report should include which of the following?
options: Functional requirements, site conditions, and design constraints
knowledgeCheck.answer: Functional requirements, site conditions, and design constraints
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The program report documents needs assessment findings. Equipment selection and wiring diagrams come during the design phase.

memorize: Six standard room typologies (A through F) and their typical AV packages
Program report components: scope, stakeholder findings, functional requirements, site survey, environmental conditions, compliance, budget, timeline, risks
understand: How master plans differ from individual room designs
Why standardization reduces TCO while still allowing room-specific customization
practice: Draft a room typology matrix for a corporate campus with 5 space types
examTraps: A master plan does NOT replace individual design — it provides the framework
Program reports don't include equipment specifications — those come in the design phase

lessons.summary: Technology master plans establish the strategic framework for enterprise AV deployment, while program reports document needs assessment findings as the bridge to design. Room typologies enable standardization at scale. The CTS-D designer creates these documents to ensure consistency, predictable budgets, and maintainable systems across large organizations.

lessons.title: Coordinating with Architects & Interior Designers
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.overview: Learn to read and interpret architectural drawings, coordinate AV requirements with architects and interior designers, and communicate design intent using construction document conventions.
learningObjectives: Read and interpret architectural floor plans, reflected ceiling plans, elevations, and sections
Understand architectural drawing scales, symbols, and conventions
Identify critical coordination points between AV design and architecture
Communicate AV space requirements, sight lines, and equipment clearances to architects
Navigate the design phases: Schematic Design (SD), Design Development (DD), and Construction Documents (CD)

keyTerms.definition: An architectural drawing showing the ceiling as if viewed from above through a transparent floor — used for speaker, projector, camera, and microphone placement.
The complete package of drawings and specifications used for bidding and building a project.
Americans with Disabilities Act — federal law requiring accessible design including assistive listening, captioning capability, and accessible controls.
The unobstructed line of vision from a viewer's seated eye height to the bottom and top of a display surface.
Early design phase establishing the overall approach, spatial relationships, and preliminary equipment locations.
Mid-phase where AV designs are refined with specific equipment selections, detailed coordination, and updated drawings.

lessons.content:
READING ARCHITECTURAL DRAWINGS

Architectural drawings are the shared language of the construction industry. A CTS-D designer must read them fluently.

DRAWING TYPES

1. Floor Plans: Top-down view showing walls, doors, furniture. AV designers add equipment locations, floor boxes, wall plates, and cable pathways.
2. Reflected Ceiling Plans (RCP): Shows ceiling as viewed from above through a transparent floor. Critical for speakers, projectors, cameras, display mounts. Ceiling grid patterns, light fixture locations, and HVAC diffusers appear here.
3. Elevations: Straight-on views of walls showing equipment mounting heights, display positions, and architectural features.
4. Sections: Cut-through views showing vertical relationships — ceiling heights, floor-to-structure dimensions, and equipment clearances.
5. Details: Enlarged views of specific construction elements — mounting brackets, wall box details, conduit routing.

SCALE AND SYMBOLS

Common architectural scales:
- 1/8" = 1'-0" (overview plans)
- 1/4" = 1'-0" (room plans — most common for AV)
- 1/2" = 1'-0" (enlarged plans)
- 1" = 1'-0" or 3" = 1'-0" (details)

Standard symbols: doors, windows, walls (solid vs. partition), electrical outlets, data outlets, dimensions, section cut indicators, elevation markers.

DESIGN PHASE COORDINATION

- Schematic Design (SD): Establish AV concepts, identify major equipment locations, define infrastructure needs. AV requirements must be communicated early — architectural changes are cheap at SD, expensive at CD.
- Design Development (DD): Refine equipment selections, coordinate exact locations with MEP, resolve conflicts with lighting and HVAC.
- Construction Documents (CD): Final AV drawings integrated into the full CD set. All equipment, pathways, power, and data locations finalized.

CRITICAL AV-ARCHITECTURE COORDINATION POINTS

1. Display wall construction: Is the wall rated to support display weight? Is power and conduit already in the wall cavity?
2. Ceiling type and height: T-bar grid (easy speaker/projector mount) vs. drywall (requires backing/blocking) vs. exposed structure
3. Window locations and daylight control: Affects display type selection and viewing angles
4. Room geometry: Parallel walls create flutter echo; irregular shapes affect speaker coverage
5. Door and furniture placement: Affects camera angles, display sight lines, and control point locations
6. Floor box locations: Must align with furniture layout and be coordinated with power/data
7. Acoustic separation: Wall construction determines sound isolation between adjacent spaces

scenarios.situation: During DD, the architect moves a conference room wall 3 feet, reducing room width from 20 to 17 feet.
scenarios.notice: This changes display sizing calculations, speaker coverage patterns, camera field of view, and potentially the entire AV system design.
scenarios.nextStep: Recalculate display size using DISCAS for the new viewing distances, verify speaker coverage, and issue a revised AV drawing set. Document the change and its impact.
scenarios.whyMatters: Architectural changes cascade through AV design. CTS-D designers must track all revisions and assess impact.

lessons.examRelevance: Task B1 (Coordination with architects/interior designers) is worth 6% of the exam. Expect questions about drawing interpretation, design phase coordination timing, and identifying AV impacts from architectural changes.

knowledgeCheck.question: At which design phase should AV infrastructure requirements first be communicated to the architect?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Infrastructure needs like conduit pathways, structural backing, and electrical requirements must be communicated at SD when changes are least costly.

knowledgeCheck.question: What type of architectural drawing shows ceiling-mounted AV equipment locations?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The RCP shows the ceiling as viewed from above — this is where projectors, speakers, cameras, and ceiling microphones are documented.

memorize: Design phases: SD → DD → CD → Construction → Closeout
Common architectural scales: 1/8", 1/4", 1/2", 1"
understand: Why early coordination (at SD) saves money vs. late changes
How to read an RCP and distinguish ceiling elements from floor elements
practice: Find architectural floor plans online and identify where AV equipment should be located
examTraps: An RCP is viewed from above looking DOWN — equipment shown is on the CEILING, not the floor
AV designers contribute to the CD set but don't produce standalone construction documents

lessons.summary: AV designers must read architectural drawings fluently and coordinate with architects starting at Schematic Design. Key coordination points include display wall construction, ceiling type, window placement, and room geometry. Changes in architectural design cascade through AV design — track all revisions and assess impact immediately.

lessons.title: MEP, Structural & IT Coordination
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.domainAlignment: Duty B — Tasks B2, B3, B4 (14%)
lessons.overview: Master coordination with Mechanical/Electrical/Plumbing engineers, structural engineers, and IT/network professionals — collectively the largest portion of Duty B and critical to successful AV system design.
learningObjectives: Calculate electrical power requirements for AV systems and communicate them to electrical engineers
Understand HVAC noise impact on AV systems and coordinate with mechanical engineers
Determine structural load requirements for displays, projectors, and speaker clusters
Coordinate AV network requirements with IT including VLANs, bandwidth, QoS, and security
Identify conduit and pathway requirements and communicate them to MEP teams

keyTerms.definition: British Thermal Units per hour — the measure of heat generated by equipment that HVAC systems must offset. Calculate: Watts × 3.412 = BTU/hr.
An electrical circuit serving only AV equipment, not shared with general building loads. Prevents noise and ensures adequate power.
NEC limits on how many cables can occupy a conduit — typically 40% fill for three or more cables.
Virtual Local Area Network — a logically segmented network. AV systems typically require a dedicated VLAN for multicast traffic isolation.
Quality of Service — network prioritization ensuring AV traffic (especially real-time audio/video) receives priority over general data traffic.
Noise Criteria — a single-number rating of acceptable background noise levels. Conference rooms typically require NC-25 to NC-30.

lessons.content:
ELECTRICAL COORDINATION (MEP-E)

AV power requirements must be communicated clearly to electrical engineers:

1. Power Calculations:
- List every AV device with its wattage
- Add 20% headroom for future expansion
- Group into circuits: don't exceed 80% of circuit capacity for continuous loads
- Example: 15A circuit at 120V = 1,800W capacity × 80% = 1,440W usable
- Example: 20A circuit at 120V = 2,400W capacity × 80% = 1,920W usable

2. Circuit Types:
- Dedicated circuits for AV racks (separate from room lighting and HVAC)
- Isolated ground circuits for sensitive audio equipment (reduces electrical noise)
- UPS-backed circuits for critical systems

3. Thermal Load:
- Every watt of AV power becomes heat that HVAC must remove
- BTU/hr = Total AV Watts × 3.412
- An AV rack consuming 2,000W generates 6,824 BTU/hr
- Communicate this to the mechanical engineer for HVAC sizing

MECHANICAL COORDINATION (MEP-M)

HVAC directly impacts AV performance:

1. Noise: HVAC is the #1 source of background noise. Supply and return diffusers near microphones create wind noise. Specify NC-25 maximum for conference rooms, NC-30 for general meeting spaces.
2. Airflow: Direct airflow on microphones causes noise. Specify diffuser placement away from ceiling microphones.
3. Thermal management: Equipment rooms need dedicated cooling. A sealed AV rack generates significant heat.
4. Vibration: Mechanical equipment on shared structures can transmit vibration to AV equipment.

STRUCTURAL COORDINATION

1. Display mounting: A 98-inch commercial display weighs 130-180 lbs. The wall must be reinforced with plywood backing or steel unistrut.
2. Projector mounting: Projectors require structural ceiling attachments — not just T-bar grid support.
3. Speaker clusters: Flown speaker arrays can weigh hundreds of pounds. Structural engineer must verify attachment points.
4. Rack rooms: Equipment racks can weigh 500-800+ lbs loaded. Floor loading capacity must be verified.

IT/NETWORK COORDINATION

1. VLAN Requirements: AV systems should have dedicated VLANs, especially for multicast traffic (video distribution, Dante audio)
2. Bandwidth: Calculate total AV bandwidth needs — a single uncompressed 4K video stream requires ~12 Gbps
3. QoS: Real-time AV traffic (especially audio) requires QoS priority. Dante audio needs DSCP EF (46) marking.
4. PoE: Many AV devices use Power over Ethernet — touch panels, cameras, ceiling mics. Verify switch PoE budget.
5. Network drops: Specify quantity and location of network ports for AV devices at each location.
6. Security: AV control systems need network access but must comply with IT security policies.

scenarios.situation: The electrical engineer asks for your AV power requirements but you haven't selected specific equipment yet (still in SD phase).
scenarios.notice: You can't provide exact wattages without equipment selection, but the electrical engineer needs circuit planning information now.
scenarios.nextStep: Provide power allowances based on room typology: 'This conference room type typically requires two dedicated 20A circuits at the AV rack location and one 20A circuit at each display location.' Refine during DD.
scenarios.whyMatters: CTS-D designers must provide useful information at each design phase, even when details aren't finalized. Waiting until CD to communicate power needs causes costly electrical redesign.

lessons.examRelevance: Tasks B2-B4 combined represent 14% of the CTS-D exam. Expect questions about power calculations, thermal load, HVAC noise criteria, structural requirements, and AV network coordination. Math questions may ask you to calculate circuit loading or BTU/hr.

workedExamples.given: AV rack with total equipment load of 1,850 watts at 120V.
workedExamples.asked: What is the minimum circuit requirement, and what is the thermal load in BTU/hr?
workedExamples.solution:
Minimum circuit: 1,850W / 120V = 15.4A. At 80% continuous load limit: 15.4A / 0.8 = 19.3A. Need a 20A circuit minimum.
Thermal load: 1,850W × 3.412 = 6,312 BTU/hr
workedExamples.answer: Minimum 20A dedicated circuit. Thermal load = 6,312 BTU/hr.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using a 15A circuit — 15A × 120V × 0.8 = 1,440W usable, which is less than the 1,850W requirement.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the maximum recommended NC rating for a conference room?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Conference rooms require NC-25 or lower for clear speech intelligibility. Higher NC ratings indicate more background noise.

knowledgeCheck.question: An AV rack consumes 3,000 watts. What thermal load must the HVAC system offset?

memorize: BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412
80% continuous load rule for circuit sizing
NC-25 for conference rooms, NC-30 for general meeting spaces
Conduit fill: 40% for 3+ cables (NEC)
understand: Why AV needs dedicated circuits and VLANs
How HVAC noise and airflow affect microphone performance
practice: Calculate power requirements for a 10-device AV rack
Determine circuit sizing for a given equipment load
examTraps: Don't forget the 80% derating for continuous loads — a 20A circuit only provides 1,920W usable
BTU calculation uses watts, not amps

lessons.summary: MEP and IT coordination represents 14% of the CTS-D exam. Key formulas: BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412, and circuits must be derated to 80% for continuous loads. HVAC noise must meet NC-25 for conference rooms. Structural verification is required for all mounted equipment. AV networks need dedicated VLANs with QoS for real-time traffic.

lessons.title: Acoustics & Life Safety Coordination
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.domainAlignment: Duty B — Tasks B5, B6, B7 (8%)
lessons.overview: Coordinate with acoustical professionals on room treatment, sound isolation, and intelligibility requirements. Understand life safety code compliance, ADA requirements, and coordination with specialty consultants.
learningObjectives: Understand reverberation time (RT60) and its impact on speech intelligibility
Interpret NC curves and specify acceptable background noise levels
Coordinate acoustic treatment recommendations with acoustical consultants
Identify ADA compliance requirements for AV systems including assistive listening
Understand plenum-rated cable requirements and fire/life safety code compliance

keyTerms.definition: Reverberation Time — the time in seconds for sound to decay by 60 dB after the source stops. Calculated using the Sabine equation: RT60 = 0.161 × V / A (metric).
Sound Transmission Class — a single-number rating of a wall or partition's ability to block sound transmission. Higher STC = better isolation.
Speech Transmission Index — a measure of speech intelligibility from 0 to 1. Above 0.60 is considered 'good' for most AV applications.
Cable with a fire-retardant jacket (CMP rating) required for installation in air-handling spaces above drop ceilings.
ADA-required system providing amplified audio to hearing-impaired users. Technologies include hearing loop (induction), RF, and IR systems.
RT60 = 0.161 × V / A, where V = room volume in cubic meters and A = total absorption in metric sabins.

lessons.content:
ACOUSTICS COORDINATION

Acoustics directly determine whether an AV system sounds good or terrible. A perfectly designed sound system in an acoustically untreated room will produce unintelligible speech.

REVERBERATION TIME (RT60)

RT60 is the single most important acoustic metric for AV designers:
- Conference rooms: 0.4 - 0.6 seconds ideal
- Training rooms: 0.6 - 0.8 seconds
- Lecture halls: 0.8 - 1.2 seconds
- Worship spaces: 1.5 - 3.0+ seconds (depends on musical vs. speech use)

Sabine Equation (metric): RT60 = 0.161 × V / A
- V = room volume in cubic meters
- A = total absorption in metric sabins (sum of all surface areas × their absorption coefficients)

High RT60 = excessive reverberation = poor speech intelligibility. If RT60 is too high, recommend acoustic treatment: absorptive ceiling tiles, wall panels, carpet, soft furnishings.

SOUND ISOLATION (STC)

STC ratings indicate how well a wall blocks sound:
- STC 30: Normal speech audible through wall
- STC 40: Loud speech faintly heard
- STC 50: Loud speech not audible — minimum for conference rooms
- STC 60: Excellent isolation — required for executive boardrooms, recording studios

Common issue: Walls may have high STC ratings, but sound leaks through HVAC ducts, ceiling plenums, electrical outlets, and door seals. The weakest link determines actual isolation.

LIFE SAFETY & CODE COMPLIANCE

1. Plenum cables: Any cable routed through air-handling spaces (above drop ceilings without ductwork) must be CMP-rated (Communications Multipurpose Plenum). Non-plenum cables in plenum spaces is a code violation.

2. Fire alarm integration: AV audio systems may need to mute or reduce volume when fire alarm activates. Some jurisdictions require AV systems to relay emergency announcements.

3. Emergency lighting: AV-controlled room lighting must not override emergency lighting requirements.

4. ADA COMPLIANCE FOR AV:
- Assistive Listening Systems (ALS): Required in assembly areas with audio amplification. Must provide receivers equal to 4% of seating capacity (minimum 2).
- ALS technologies: Hearing loop (induction), RF, IR — each has pros/cons
- Control height: Touch panels and controls must be accessible (15-48 inches AFF per ADA)
- Visual indicators: Systems providing audio cues should also provide visual notification
- Captioning capability: Consider closed captioning for video content

5. Seismic requirements: In seismic zones, all ceiling-mounted equipment must meet seismic bracing requirements (varies by jurisdiction).

scenarios.situation: A client's new conference room has all glass walls and a polished concrete floor. They report echo is terrible.
scenarios.notice: Glass and concrete are highly reflective surfaces with very low absorption coefficients. RT60 is likely well above 1.0 second.
scenarios.nextStep: Calculate RT60 and recommend acoustic treatment: acoustic panels on at least two walls, absorptive ceiling treatment, and area rugs or carpet. Coordinate with the interior designer on aesthetically acceptable treatment options.
scenarios.whyMatters: No amount of DSP processing can fully compensate for a reverberant room. Acoustic treatment is always the first solution — electronic correction is supplementary.

lessons.examRelevance: Tasks B5-B7 combined represent 8% of the CTS-D exam. The Sabine equation for RT60 calculation is a common exam math question. Expect questions about STC ratings, ADA assistive listening requirements, and plenum cable requirements.

workedExamples.given: Conference room: 8m long × 6m wide × 3m ceiling height. Total absorption = 45 metric sabins.
workedExamples.asked: Calculate the RT60 using the Sabine equation.
workedExamples.answer: RT60 = 0.52 seconds — within the ideal range (0.4-0.6s) for conference rooms.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using room area instead of volume: 8 × 6 = 48, not 144. The Sabine equation requires VOLUME (L × W × H).

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the ideal RT60 range for a conference room?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Conference rooms need short RT60 for clear speech. Too short feels 'dead'; too long creates echo and reduces intelligibility.

knowledgeCheck.question: ADA requires assistive listening receivers equal to what percentage of seating capacity?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ADA requires receivers equal to 4% of total seating capacity, with a minimum of 2 receivers regardless of room size.

memorize: Sabine equation: RT60 = 0.161 × V / A (metric)
RT60 targets: conference 0.4-0.6s, training 0.6-0.8s, lecture 0.8-1.2s
STC-50 minimum for conference rooms
ADA ALS: 4% of seats, minimum 2 receivers
Plenum cable = CMP rating
understand: Why acoustic treatment is always preferable to electronic correction
How sound leaks through the weakest element (duct, outlet, door seal)
practice: Calculate RT60 for rooms of various sizes using the Sabine equation
examTraps: Sabine equation uses VOLUME, not area
STC rating of a wall is irrelevant if sound leaks through the ceiling plenum above it

lessons.summary: Acoustics coordination focuses on RT60 (Sabine equation), sound isolation (STC), and intelligibility (STI). Life safety requires plenum-rated cables, fire alarm integration, and ADA compliance including assistive listening at 4% of seating capacity. The CTS-D designer coordinates with acousticians but must understand the fundamentals to make informed design decisions.

lessons.title: AV Math Fundamentals: Power, Decibels & Inverse Square Law
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.overview: Master the essential AV math formulas used throughout the CTS-D exam: Ohm's Law, power calculations, decibel math (power and voltage), the inverse square law, and constant-voltage speaker calculations.
learningObjectives: Apply Ohm's Law and power formulas to AV circuit calculations
Calculate decibel values for both power ratios (10 log) and voltage/distance ratios (20 log)
Apply the inverse square law to predict SPL changes with distance
Calculate amplifier power requirements for constant-voltage (70V/100V) speaker systems
Use the throw ratio formula for projector lens selection

keyTerms.definition: V = I × R. Voltage equals current (amps) times resistance (ohms). The foundation of all electrical calculations.
A logarithmic unit expressing the ratio between two values. Power: dB = 10 × log(P1/P2). Voltage/distance: dB = 20 × log(V1/V2).
Sound pressure level drops 6 dB for every doubling of distance from a point source in free field.
The ratio of throw distance to image width: TR = D / W. Used for projector lens selection.
A distributed speaker system using 25V, 70V, or 100V line. Total wattage = sum of all speaker tap settings. Amplifier must exceed this total.
Number of Open Microphones — each doubling of open mics reduces system gain before feedback by 3 dB.

lessons.content:
CORE AV MATH — YOUR EXAM FORMULA SHEET IS PROVIDED

You DON'T need to memorize these formulas — they're on the exam reference sheet. You DO need to know WHEN to use each one and HOW to solve them.

OHM'S LAW & POWER

V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance)
P = V × I (Power = Voltage × Current)
P = I² × R
P = V² / R

These are used for circuit sizing, speaker impedance calculations, and amplifier loading.

DECIBEL MATH

Two formulas — know which to use:
- Power ratio: dB = 10 × log(P1/P2) — used for amplifier power comparisons
- Voltage/distance ratio: dB = 20 × log(V1/V2) or 20 × log(D1/D2) — used for SPL changes with distance

Key dB relationships:
- Double power = +3 dB
- 10× power = +10 dB
- Double voltage = +6 dB
- Double distance = -6 dB (inverse square law)

INVERSE SQUARE LAW

For a point source in free field (no reflections):
SPL drops 6 dB for every doubling of distance.

If SPL is 90 dB at 1 meter:
- 2 meters: 84 dB
- 4 meters: 78 dB
- 8 meters: 72 dB
- 16 meters: 66 dB

Formula: SPL₂ = SPL₁ - 20 × log(D₂/D₁)

CONSTANT-VOLTAGE SPEAKER SYSTEMS

70V (or 100V) distributed speaker systems:
1. Each speaker has a transformer with selectable watt taps (e.g., 1W, 2W, 4W, 8W)
2. Total load = sum of all tap settings
3. Amplifier must provide: Total load × 1.5 (50% headroom)
4. Maximum speakers on a 70V system: limited by total watt tap sum not exceeding amplifier rating

THROW RATIO

Throw Ratio = Throw Distance / Image Width

Used to select projector lenses:
- Short throw: TR < 1.0
- Standard throw: TR 1.5 - 2.5
- Long throw: TR > 2.5

Example: Room requires 10-foot wide image. Projector will be mounted 20 feet from screen.
TR = 20 / 10 = 2.0 — select a lens with a throw ratio range that includes 2.0

workedExamples.given: A loudspeaker produces 94 dB SPL at 1 meter.
workedExamples.asked: What is the SPL at 8 meters?
workedExamples.solution:
Distance ratio: 8/1 = 8. That's 3 doublings (1→2→4→8).
Each doubling = -6 dB. So: 3 × -6 = -18 dB.
SPL at 8m = 94 - 18 = 76 dB.
Or by formula: SPL = 94 - 20 × log(8/1) = 94 - 20 × 0.903 = 94 - 18.06 = 75.94 dB ≈ 76 dB
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using 10 × log instead of 20 × log — that's for power ratios, not distance.

workedExamples.given: A 70V distributed audio system has 12 speakers, each tapped at 4 watts.
workedExamples.asked: What is the minimum amplifier power required?
workedExamples.solution:
Total load = 12 speakers × 4W = 48W
With 50% headroom: 48W × 1.5 = 72W
Select the next available amplifier size ≥ 72W
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Forgetting the 1.5× headroom multiplier and specifying a 50W amplifier — insufficient for peak demands and system longevity.

workedExamples.given: A conference room needs a 12-foot wide projected image. The projector mount is 22 feet from the screen.
workedExamples.asked: What throw ratio lens is needed?
workedExamples.answer: TR = 1.83 — select a standard throw lens with a range that includes 1.83 (e.g., 1.5-2.0:1)
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Dividing width by distance (12/22 = 0.55) — that gives the inverse of throw ratio.

lessons.examRelevance: Math questions appear across all duties. The formula sheet is provided, but you must know which formula to apply. Common exam questions: inverse square law distance/SPL calculations, amplifier sizing for 70V systems, throw ratio for projectors, circuit loading calculations, and dB conversions.

knowledgeCheck.question: If you double the power to a speaker, how much does the SPL increase?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Doubling power = +3 dB (10 × log(2) = 3.01). This is a power ratio, so use the 10 × log formula.

knowledgeCheck.question: A projector mounted 15 feet from a screen must produce a 10-foot wide image. What throw ratio lens is needed?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Throw Ratio = Distance / Width = 15 / 10 = 1.5:1

memorize: dB power: 10 × log(ratio). dB voltage/distance: 20 × log(ratio)
Double power = +3 dB. Double voltage = +6 dB. Double distance = -6 dB
70V amplifier sizing: total taps × 1.5
Throw ratio = distance / width
understand: When to use 10×log vs 20×log
Why inverse square law uses 20×log (because SPL is a pressure/voltage quantity, not power)
practice: Calculate SPL at various distances from a known source
Size amplifiers for 70V speaker systems with different tap configurations
examTraps: Distance uses 20 × log, not 10 × log — because SPL is a pressure measurement
Throw ratio is distance/width, NOT width/distance
studyNotes.fieldTip: When in doubt on the exam, check units. If the question involves power (watts), use 10×log. If it involves voltage, pressure, or distance, use 20×log.

lessons.summary: AV math on the CTS-D exam requires knowing WHEN to apply each formula, not memorizing them. Key relationships: double power = +3 dB (10×log), double distance = -6 dB SPL (20×log), throw ratio = distance/width, and 70V amplifier sizing = total taps × 1.5. The formula sheet is provided — practice applying the formulas to scenarios.

lessons.title: AV Project Lifecycle & Design Phases
lessons.module: Day 1: Foundations — Needs Analysis, Coordination & AV Math
lessons.domainAlignment: Duty A, B, C, D — Process Framework
lessons.overview: Understand the complete AV project lifecycle from initial consultation through closeout, and how the CTS-D designer's responsibilities align with each phase of the construction process.
learningObjectives: Describe the four AV project phases: Program, Design, Construction, Verification
Identify CTS-D designer responsibilities at each phase
Understand how AV design phases align with architectural SD, DD, and CD phases
Recognize the importance of scope management and change order processes
Describe the transition from design to deployment including shop drawings and submittals

keyTerms.definition: Detailed fabrication and installation drawings created by the AV integrator based on the designer's construction documents. Must be reviewed and approved by the designer.
Documentation provided by the integrator for designer approval — includes product data sheets, shop drawings, and samples.
Request for Information — a formal question from the integrator to the designer seeking clarification on design intent or resolving ambiguities.
A formal modification to the project scope, schedule, or budget — must be documented, priced, and approved before work proceeds.
A list of incomplete or deficient items identified during final walkthrough that must be resolved before project acceptance.
The systematic process of verifying that installed AV systems meet design intent and performance specifications.

lessons.content:
THE AV PROJECT LIFECYCLE

Four phases define the AV project lifecycle. The CTS-D designer's involvement spans all four but is heaviest in the first three.

PHASE 1: PROGRAM (Duty A)

Activities:
- Initial client consultation and stakeholder interviews
- Needs assessment and functional requirements gathering
- Site survey and existing conditions documentation
- Program report development
- Preliminary budget development
- Technology master plan (if applicable)

Deliverables: Program Report, Technology Master Plan

PHASE 2: DESIGN (Duties B & C)

Sub-phases aligned with architecture:

Schematic Design (SD) — 30% Design:
- Conceptual AV design and equipment layouts
- Preliminary signal flow diagrams
- Infrastructure requirements communicated to architect and MEP
- Preliminary equipment budgets

Design Development (DD) — 60% Design:
- Equipment selection and specification
- Detailed signal flow and system block diagrams
- Coordination with all allied trades
- Room acoustic analysis and recommendations
- Control system architecture
- Network requirements documentation

Construction Documents (CD) — 100% Design:
- Final AV drawings (floor plans, RCPs, elevations, details)
- Equipment schedules and Bill of Materials
- Cable schedules
- Rack elevation drawings
- Written specifications (CSI format)
- Complete bid package

PHASE 3: CONSTRUCTION (Duties C & D)

Activities:
- Review shop drawings and submittals from integrator
- Respond to RFIs
- Conduct site visits during rough-in and trim-out
- Review change orders for scope and budget impact
- Coordinate with CM/GC on scheduling

PHASE 4: VERIFICATION (Duty D)

Activities:
- System commissioning and performance verification
- Testing against design specifications (AVIXA standards)
- Punch list walkthrough
- End-user training
- As-built documentation review
- O&M manual compilation
- Project closeout and warranty handoff

SCOPE MANAGEMENT

Scope creep is the #1 cause of AV project problems. Every change must follow the change order process:
1. Client requests change
2. Designer evaluates impact (cost, schedule, other systems)
3. Change order document prepared with pricing
4. Client approves in writing
5. Design documents updated
6. Construction proceeds with revised scope

scenarios.situation: During construction, the general contractor asks the AV integrator to relocate a floor box 6 feet from its documented position.
scenarios.notice: This is a change to the AV design that wasn't initiated by the designer or client. It may affect cable lengths, conduit routing, and furniture coordination.
scenarios.nextStep: The integrator should submit an RFI to the AV designer before making the change. The designer evaluates impact and issues a response — either approving with modifications or rejecting with explanation.
scenarios.whyMatters: Unauthorized changes during construction can create design conflicts. The CTS-D designer is responsible for maintaining design integrity through the shop drawing and RFI process.

lessons.examRelevance: Understanding the project lifecycle is tested across all four duties. Questions will ask what deliverables belong to which phase, when specific coordination activities should occur, and the proper process for handling changes during construction.

knowledgeCheck.question: At which design sub-phase should final AV equipment selections be made?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: DD is when equipment is selected and specified. SD uses conceptual/preliminary selections. CD finalizes documentation based on DD decisions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Who reviews and approves shop drawings from the AV integrator?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The AV designer reviews shop drawings to verify they match design intent. This is a core CTS-D responsibility during the construction phase.

memorize: Four phases: Program → Design → Construction → Verification
Design sub-phases: SD (30%) → DD (60%) → CD (100%)
Change order process: request → evaluate → document → approve → update → construct
understand: Why early coordination (SD) is cheaper than late changes (CD/Construction)
The relationship between shop drawings, submittals, and RFIs
practice: Map each CTS-D duty to its primary project phase(s)
examTraps: Equipment selection happens at DD, not CD — CD is for documentation, not decision-making
Shop drawings are created by the integrator, not the designer — the designer REVIEWS them

lessons.summary: The AV project lifecycle spans four phases: Program (needs assessment), Design (SD→DD→CD), Construction (shop drawing review, RFIs, site visits), and Verification (commissioning, closeout). The CTS-D designer's responsibilities shift from gathering requirements to creating designs to reviewing implementation to verifying performance. Scope management through proper change order processes is critical.

lessons.title: Display Systems Design & AVIXA DISCAS Standard
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Master display image sizing using the AVIXA DISCAS standard (V202.01), including viewing distance calculations, display technology selection, and the critical design decisions between flat panel displays, projection, and LED video walls.
learningObjectives: Apply AVIXA V202.01 (DISCAS) to determine minimum display size for basic and analytical decision making
Calculate viewing distances using the 4H/6H/8H guidelines
Compare display technologies: LCD, LED direct-view, projection (DLP, LCD, laser), OLED
Determine when to specify flat panel vs. projection vs. LED video wall
Calculate screen aspect ratios and their impact on content display

keyTerms.definition: Display Image Size for 2D Content in Audiovisual Systems — AVIXA standard V202.01 defining minimum image sizes based on viewer distance and content type.
DISCAS category for content requiring general understanding (video, graphics). Maximum viewing distance = 8× image height.
DISCAS category for content requiring detailed reading (spreadsheets, small text). Maximum viewing distance = 4× image height.
A measure of a projection screen's reflectivity compared to a standard reference (1.0). Higher gain = brighter center image but narrower viewing angle.
The distance in millimeters between LED pixel centers on a direct-view LED display. Smaller pitch = higher resolution at closer viewing distances.
The ratio of the brightest white to the darkest black a display can produce. AVIXA V201.01 defines system contrast ratio including ambient light.

lessons.content:
DISPLAY IMAGE SIZING — AVIXA V202.01 (DISCAS)

DISCAS is THE standard for determining display size. It defines two content categories:

1. Basic Decision Making (BDM): Video, graphics, presentations with large text
   - Maximum viewing distance: 8× image height (8H)
   - Minimum image height: Farthest viewer distance / 8

2. Analytical Decision Making (ADM): Spreadsheets, CAD, small text
   - Maximum viewing distance: 4× image height (4H)
   - Minimum image height: Farthest viewer distance / 4

Many designers also reference 6H as a middle ground for mixed content.

DISPLAY SIZING CALCULATION

Step 1: Measure the farthest viewer distance from the display
Step 2: Determine content type (BDM or ADM)
Step 3: Calculate minimum image height: Distance / multiplier
Step 4: Select display size that provides at least that image height

16:9 display measurements (diagonal to height conversion):
- 55" display: ~27" (69cm) image height
- 65" display: ~32" (81cm) image height
- 75" display: ~37" (94cm) image height
- 85" display: ~42" (107cm) image height
- 98" display: ~48" (122cm) image height

DISPLAY TECHNOLOGY COMPARISON

LCD Flat Panel:
- Sizes: 43" to 98" typical commercial
- Best for: Conference rooms, huddle spaces, digital signage
- Pros: Bright (500+ nits), good in ambient light, low maintenance
- Cons: Limited to ~98" maximum size, bezels in tiled configurations

Direct-View LED:
- Sizes: Virtually unlimited (modular panels)
- Pixel pitch: 0.7mm to 4.0mm+ (smaller = higher resolution)
- Best for: Large venues, lobbies, command centers, any size requirement > 98"
- Pros: Seamless, extremely bright, long lifespan, scalable
- Cons: High cost, minimum viewing distance based on pixel pitch
- Rule of thumb: Minimum viewing distance ≈ pixel pitch (mm) × 8 (in feet)

Projection:
- Image sizes: 80" to 300"+ (limited by light output vs. screen size)
- Technologies: DLP, LCD, LCoS, laser illumination
- Best for: Large images on budget, temporary installations, rear projection
- Pros: Large image size, lower cost than equivalent LED
- Cons: Requires light control, lamp/laser maintenance, throw distance requirements
- Throw ratio: TR = Distance / Width

OLED:
- Sizes: 55" to 97"
- Best for: Executive spaces requiring superior image quality
- Pros: Perfect black levels, wide viewing angle, thin profile
- Cons: Risk of image retention, lower brightness than LCD, higher cost

SYSTEM CONTRAST RATIO (AVIXA V201.01)

Displays are measured by their system contrast ratio, which accounts for ambient light:
- The room's ambient light reduces the effective contrast ratio
- Projection systems are most affected — bright rooms kill contrast
- Direct-view displays (LCD, LED, OLED) handle ambient light better
- Design principle: If you can't control the light, don't use projection

workedExamples.given: Conference room 30 feet deep. Farthest viewer sits 28 feet from the display wall. Content includes spreadsheets and financial data.
workedExamples.asked: What is the minimum display image height? What display size is needed?
workedExamples.solution:
Content type: Analytical Decision Making (spreadsheets) = 4H rule
Minimum image height = 28 feet / 4 = 7 feet = 84 inches
A single flat panel cannot achieve 84" image height (98" display = 48" height).
Options: Dual 98" displays stacked, direct-view LED wall, or projection with 84"+ tall screen.
workedExamples.answer: 84" minimum image height. A single flat panel is insufficient. Recommend a direct-view LED wall or dual-display configuration.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using the 8H rule (BDM) instead of 4H (ADM) for spreadsheet content would yield only 42" minimum height — a single 98" display would seem adequate but viewers couldn't read the data.

workedExamples.given: Presentation room needs an 8-foot (96") wide projected image. Projector mount location is 14 feet from screen.
workedExamples.asked: What throw ratio lens is required?
workedExamples.answer: TR = 1.75:1 — standard throw lens. Select a projector with a zoom range that includes 1.75.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Measuring throw distance to screen CENTER instead of screen SURFACE — throw distance is always measured to the projection surface.

lessons.examRelevance: DISCAS display sizing is one of the most commonly tested topics on the CTS-D exam. Expect 4-6 questions involving 4H/6H/8H calculations, display technology selection based on room conditions, and throw ratio calculations for projection systems.

knowledgeCheck.question: Using DISCAS, what is the maximum viewing distance for analytical decision making on a display with a 40-inch image height?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ADM = 4H rule. Maximum distance = 4 × 40 inches = 160 inches = 13.3 feet.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which display technology is most affected by ambient room lighting?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Projection relies on reflected light — ambient light washes out the image and destroys contrast ratio. Self-emissive displays (LCD, LED, OLED) handle ambient light much better.

memorize: DISCAS: BDM = 8H, ADM = 4H, mixed = 6H
Throw ratio = distance / width
LED minimum viewing: pixel pitch (mm) × 8 ≈ feet
understand: Why ADM requires a closer viewing distance (4H) than BDM (8H)
How ambient light affects different display technologies differently
practice: Calculate display sizes for rooms of various depths with both BDM and ADM content
examTraps: DISCAS uses image HEIGHT, not diagonal size
Throw ratio uses image WIDTH, not height — don't mix up H and W

lessons.summary: DISCAS (V202.01) is the cornerstone of AV display design. Use 4H for analytical content (spreadsheets), 8H for basic content (video), and 6H for mixed use. Always calculate from the FARTHEST viewer. Display technology selection depends on room size, ambient light, and content type. Projection requires light control; flat panels max out at 98"; LED walls scale infinitely but cost more.

lessons.title: Video Signal Types, Distribution & AV-over-IP
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Understand all video signal formats, bandwidth requirements, and distribution methods from point-to-point HDMI through enterprise-scale AV-over-IP systems. Learn to select the right transport technology for each design scenario.
learningObjectives: Compare video signal formats: HDMI, DisplayPort, SDI, HDBaseT, and fiber optic
Calculate video bandwidth requirements for various resolutions
Design video distribution systems using matrix switching, HDBaseT, and AV-over-IP
Understand compression standards (H.264, H.265) and their impact on quality and bandwidth
Select appropriate video transport technology based on distance, bandwidth, and infrastructure

keyTerms.definition: High-Definition Multimedia Interface — carries uncompressed video + audio. V2.0: 18 Gbps (4K@60). V2.1: 48 Gbps (8K@60). Max cable: ~15m passive, longer with active cables.
Uncompressed 4K video, audio, Ethernet, control, and PoE over a single Cat6/6A cable up to 100 meters.
Serial Digital Interface — broadcast-standard video. HD-SDI: 1.485 Gbps. 3G-SDI: 2.97 Gbps. 12G-SDI: 11.88 Gbps (4K@60). Coax, up to 100m+.
Audio/video distribution using standard IP network infrastructure. Enables scalable, switch-based routing over existing Ethernet networks.
Reducing color resolution to save bandwidth. 4:4:4 = full color (best). 4:2:2 = half horizontal color. 4:2:0 = quarter color (used in most consumer video).
Extended Display Identification Data — information exchanged between source and display to establish supported resolutions and capabilities.

lessons.content:
VIDEO SIGNAL FORMATS

HDMI (Most Common in Commercial AV):
- HDMI 1.4: 10.2 Gbps — 4K@30Hz or 1080p@60Hz
- HDMI 2.0: 18 Gbps — 4K@60Hz 4:2:0 or 4K@30Hz 4:4:4
- HDMI 2.1: 48 Gbps — 8K@60Hz, 4K@120Hz
- Maximum cable length: ~5m (passive 4K), 15m with active cables
- Supports: video + audio + CEC + ARC + Ethernet (HEC)

DisplayPort:
- DP 1.2: 17.28 Gbps — 4K@60Hz
- DP 1.4: 25.92 Gbps — 8K@30Hz, 4K@120Hz
- DP 2.0: 77.37 Gbps
- Primarily used in PC/workstation environments
- USB-C Alt Mode carries DisplayPort signal

SDI (Broadcast/Production):
- HD-SDI: 1.485 Gbps — 1080i/720p
- 3G-SDI: 2.97 Gbps — 1080p@60
- 6G-SDI: 5.94 Gbps — 4K@30
- 12G-SDI: 11.88 Gbps — 4K@60
- Uses BNC coax connectors, up to 100m+ (varies by data rate)
- Unidirectional — no EDID handshake issues

VIDEO DISTRIBUTION METHODS

1. Point-to-Point: Direct HDMI/DP cable. Simple but limited distance.
2. Matrix Switching: Central switch routes any input to any output. HDMI matrix (short distance) or HDBaseT matrix (up to 100m per output).
3. HDBaseT Distribution: Extends uncompressed 4K up to 100m over Cat6/6A. Transmitter at source, receiver at display. Great for medium-scale systems (4-32 endpoints).
4. AV-over-IP: Encoder at each source, decoder at each display, all connected to a managed Ethernet switch. Infinitely scalable. Uses standard network infrastructure.

AV-OVER-IP APPROACHES

- Uncompressed (e.g., SDVoE): Zero latency, requires 10GbE infrastructure. ~9 Gbps per 4K stream.
- Visually Lossless (e.g., many proprietary codecs): Near-zero latency, 1GbE capable. Slight compression not visible to eye.
- Compressed (H.264/H.265): Low bandwidth (~20-50 Mbps for 4K), works on existing 1GbE. Introduces 1-2 frame latency. Best for digital signage and soft-codec conferencing.

BANDWIDTH CALCULATIONS

Uncompressed video bandwidth:
Bandwidth = H_pixels × V_pixels × frame_rate × color_depth × 3 (for RGB)

1080p@60 = 1920 × 1080 × 60 × 8 × 3 = 2.99 Gbps
4K@60 (4:4:4) = 3840 × 2160 × 60 × 8 × 3 = 11.94 Gbps
4K@60 (4:2:0) = ~5.97 Gbps (half the color data)
8K@60 = ~47.78 Gbps

scenarios.situation: A corporate campus needs video distribution to 80 displays across 4 buildings with distances up to 300 meters.
scenarios.notice: HDBaseT maxes out at 100m. HDMI maxes out at ~15m. The scale (80 endpoints) and distance (300m) exceeds traditional matrix switching.
scenarios.nextStep: Design an AV-over-IP system using the campus IP network. Encoder at each source, decoder at each display, managed switches with IGMP snooping and QoS. For 300m distances, standard Ethernet with fiber uplinks between buildings.
scenarios.whyMatters: AV-over-IP is the only practical solution at this scale and distance. CTS-D designers must recognize when traditional point-to-point or matrix solutions are insufficient.

lessons.examRelevance: Video signal types and distribution methods are heavily tested in Duty C. Expect questions comparing HDMI vs. HDBaseT vs. SDI capabilities, bandwidth calculations, and when to specify AV-over-IP vs. traditional switching.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the maximum transmission distance for HDBaseT over Cat6A?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: HDBaseT can transmit uncompressed 4K video, audio, Ethernet, control, and PoE up to 100 meters over a single Cat6/6A cable.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which video transport is unidirectional and does not use EDID handshaking?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: SDI is a broadcast standard that transmits in one direction without EDID negotiation, making it very reliable for production environments.

memorize: HDMI 2.0 = 18 Gbps (4K@60), HDBaseT = 100m over Cat6, SDI = BNC coax broadcast
AV-over-IP: uncompressed (10GbE), visually lossless (1GbE), compressed (H.264/265)
understand: Why AV-over-IP scales better than matrix switching for large systems
The trade-off between bandwidth and compression/latency
practice: Design a video distribution system for a 20-room facility choosing the appropriate transport technology
examTraps: HDBaseT distance is 100m from transmitter to receiver, not total cable run including patch panels
HDMI 2.0 supports 4K@60 only at 4:2:0 chroma — 4:4:4 requires HDMI 2.1 at 4K@60

lessons.summary: Video signal selection depends on distance, bandwidth, scale, and infrastructure. HDMI for short runs, HDBaseT for up to 100m, SDI for broadcast, and AV-over-IP for enterprise scale. Uncompressed 4K@60 requires ~12 Gbps bandwidth. AV-over-IP enables infinite scalability using standard Ethernet infrastructure but introduces compression/latency trade-offs.

lessons.title: Audio System Design: Speakers, Microphones & DSP
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Design complete audio systems including loudspeaker selection and coverage, microphone types and placement, DSP architecture, and the critical calculations for sound reinforcement including PAG/NAG analysis.
learningObjectives: Select appropriate loudspeaker types based on room geometry and coverage requirements
Design constant-voltage (70V/100V) distributed speaker systems with proper amplifier sizing
Choose microphone types and placement based on application requirements
Understand DSP signal flow and processing chain architecture
Calculate Potential Acoustic Gain (PAG) and Needed Acoustic Gain (NAG) for sound reinforcement

keyTerms.definition: The angle at which a loudspeaker's SPL drops 6 dB from on-axis. Defines the useful coverage area. Specified as horizontal × vertical (e.g., 90° × 60°).
Potential Acoustic Gain — the maximum gain a sound system can achieve before feedback. Determined by distances between source, microphone, loudspeaker, and listener.
Needed Acoustic Gain — the gain required for the farthest listener to hear as clearly as the nearest listener to the natural source.
Digital Signal Processor — processes audio signals including EQ, mixing, routing, echo cancellation, noise reduction, and automatic gain control.
Acoustic Echo Cancellation — DSP function that removes speaker audio from microphone signals during video conferencing to prevent echo.
Multiple microphone capsules in a ceiling-mounted unit that use beamforming to focus pickup on talkers while rejecting noise.

lessons.content:
LOUDSPEAKER DESIGN

Speaker Types for AV Systems:

1. Ceiling Speakers (most common in commercial AV):
- Used in: conference rooms, classrooms, open offices
- Coverage: typically 90°-120° conical dispersion
- Mounting: in-ceiling (requires ceiling cavity), pendant mount, surface mount
- Constant voltage (70V/100V) for distributed systems

2. Surface/Wall-Mount Speakers:
- Used in: conference rooms, small to medium venues
- Directional coverage for specific audience areas
- Low impedance (4-8Ω) or constant voltage

3. Column/Line Array Speakers:
- Used in: large conference rooms, worship, lecture halls
- Narrow vertical coverage, wide horizontal
- Excellent for long throw and reverberant spaces
- Steerable beam technology available

CONSTANT-VOLTAGE SPEAKER SYSTEMS (70V / 100V)

Design steps:
1. Determine coverage area and number of speakers needed
2. Select watt tap for each speaker based on required SPL
3. Sum all watt taps = total system load
4. Amplifier power = total load × 1.5 (headroom)
5. Verify total load doesn't exceed amplifier rating

MICROPHONE SELECTION

Types and applications:
- Ceiling microphone arrays: Best for conference rooms. Beamforming technology. No table clutter.
- Tabletop boundary microphones: Omnidirectional, low profile. Good for small groups.
- Gooseneck microphones: Podium, lectern, council chambers. Cardioid or supercardioid.
- Lapel/lavalier: Presenters, lecturers. Requires wireless system.
- Handheld wireless: Presentations, audience Q&A. Dynamic or condenser.

Critical design rule: Minimize the number of open microphones. Each doubling of open mics = -3 dB system gain before feedback (NOM penalty).

DSP ARCHITECTURE

Signal flow chain:
Microphones → Input gain → AEC → Noise gate → Compressor → EQ → Mixer → Output routing → Amplifier → Speakers

Key DSP functions:
- Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC): Essential for any room with speakers and microphones (video conferencing)
- Automatic Gain Control (AGC): Maintains consistent levels despite varying talker distances
- Noise gate: Mutes inactive microphones to reduce NOM
- Feedback suppression: Notch filters that detect and suppress feedback frequencies
- Room EQ: Corrects frequency response for room acoustics
- Delay: Time-aligns distributed speakers with the main source

PAG / NAG ANALYSIS

Potential Acoustic Gain (PAG) = the maximum gain the system can deliver before feedback:
PAG = 20×log(D1) - 20×log(D2) + 20×log(D0) - 20×log(DS) - 10×log(NOM) - FSM

Where:
- D1 = distance from loudspeaker to farthest listener
- D2 = distance from loudspeaker to nearest open microphone
- D0 = distance from talker to nearest microphone
- DS = distance from talker to farthest listener (without reinforcement)
- NOM = number of open microphones
- FSM = feedback stability margin (typically 6 dB)

Needed Acoustic Gain (NAG) = gain required so farthest listener hears as well as closest:
NAG = 20×log(DS) - 20×log(D0)

Design rule: PAG must be ≥ NAG for the system to work without feedback.

workedExamples.given: Conference room 70V speaker system: 8 ceiling speakers tapped at 2W each, plus 2 ceiling speakers tapped at 4W each.
workedExamples.solution:
Total load = (8 × 2W) + (2 × 4W) = 16 + 8 = 24W
With 50% headroom: 24W × 1.5 = 36W
Select next available size ≥ 36W
workedExamples.answer: Minimum 36W amplifier — specify a 40W or 60W model.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Adding speakers (8+2=10) instead of watt taps, or forgetting the 1.5× headroom multiplier.

lessons.examRelevance: Audio system design is a core Duty C topic. Expect questions on speaker system sizing (70V calculations), microphone selection, DSP signal chain, and PAG/NAG analysis. Math questions will involve amplifier sizing and NOM calculations.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens to system gain before feedback when the number of open microphones doubles?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Each doubling of NOM (Number of Open Microphones) reduces potential acoustic gain by 3 dB. This is why auto-mixing and noise gates are critical.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a DSP signal chain for video conferencing, where should AEC be placed?
options: Before all other processing, right after input gain
knowledgeCheck.answer: Before all other processing, right after input gain
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AEC must process the raw microphone signal to effectively cancel speaker audio. Other processing (EQ, compression) would alter the signal and reduce AEC effectiveness.

memorize: 70V amp sizing: sum all taps × 1.5
NOM penalty: each doubling = -3 dB gain
DSP chain: Input → AEC → Gate → Comp → EQ → Mix → Output
PAG must be ≥ NAG
understand: Why ceiling mic arrays with beamforming are preferred for modern conference rooms
How NOM reduction (auto-mixing) improves system gain and intelligibility
practice: Size a 70V amplifier for a distributed ceiling speaker system
Design a DSP signal flow for a conference room with video conferencing
examTraps: 70V amplifier sizing uses WATT TAPS, not number of speakers
AEC must be first in the processing chain — after other processing it can't effectively cancel

lessons.summary: Audio system design covers speaker selection (ceiling, surface, column array), constant-voltage system sizing (sum taps × 1.5), microphone selection (minimize NOM), and DSP architecture (AEC first in chain). PAG must exceed NAG for sound reinforcement to work without feedback. Each doubling of open microphones costs 3 dB of system gain.

lessons.title: Control Systems Design
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Design AV control system architectures including processor selection, control interfaces, user interface design, and the integration of diverse control protocols (RS-232, IR, IP, relay) into a unified system.
learningObjectives: Define control system architecture based on room complexity and user requirements
Identify control protocols: RS-232, IR, IP/TCP, relay, CEC, and their appropriate uses
Design user interfaces that match end-user skill levels
Specify control points: touch panels, keypads, scheduling panels, mobile apps
Understand control system programming documentation requirements

keyTerms.definition: The central brain of an AV control system that executes programmed logic, communicates with devices, and responds to user input.
Serial communication protocol. Point-to-point, 2-wire (TX/RX). Used for projector control, display control, and legacy devices. Max ~15m without extender.
Line-of-sight control using infrared light. Used for consumer devices without serial/IP ports. Requires IR emitter placement on device sensor.
An electrically operated switch. Used to control screen drops, lifts, shades, and lighting circuits. Can control high-voltage devices safely.
A display mounted outside meeting rooms showing availability, allowing ad-hoc booking, and integrating with calendar systems (Outlook, Google, etc.).
A programmed sequence of commands triggered by a single user action (e.g., 'Start Meeting' powers on display, lowers screen, sets lighting, starts video call).

lessons.content:
CONTROL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

Control complexity tiers:

Tier 1 — No Control System:
- Direct device control via remote/OSD
- Consumer-grade USB conferencing (Zoom/Teams room kit)
- Appropriate for huddle rooms and simple spaces

Tier 2 — Simple Control:
- Keypad or small touch panel
- Basic source switching, volume, display on/off
- Pre-programmed macros: 'Start Meeting,' 'End Meeting'
- Appropriate for standard conference rooms

Tier 3 — Full Control System:
- Touch panel(s) with custom GUI
- Central processor with multi-device control
- Room combining, complex routing, lighting integration
- Appropriate for boardrooms, training centers, event spaces

Tier 4 — Enterprise Control:
- Networked control across multiple rooms
- Central monitoring and management
- Room analytics and utilization reporting
- Help desk remote access
- Appropriate for campus-wide deployments

CONTROL PROTOCOLS

RS-232 Serial:
- Most reliable for display/projector power on/off
- Point-to-point wiring required
- Baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits must match device settings
- Maximum distance: ~15m (50 feet) without extender

IP/TCP Control:
- Devices with Ethernet: control via API, Telnet, HTTP
- Enables control over existing network infrastructure
- Bidirectional — can query device status
- Requires network connectivity and device IP management

IR (Infrared):
- Last resort when no serial or IP control is available
- Requires IR emitter physically attached to device sensor
- One-way — no feedback on command execution
- Common for legacy cable boxes, satellite receivers

Relay:
- Controls physical devices: motorized screens, shades, lifts
- Simple on/off or momentary contact
- Requires appropriate voltage and current ratings

USER INTERFACE DESIGN

Principles for AV touch panel design:
1. Simplicity first — 80% of users need 3-4 buttons maximum
2. One-touch start: 'Start Meeting' macro handles all power-on, routing, and defaults
3. Consistent layout across all rooms in an organization
4. Clear visual feedback showing system state
5. Volume control with clear mute indicator
6. Help/IT contact button
7. 'End Meeting' or 'All Off' button prominently placed
8. Advanced functions accessible but not prominent

scenarios.situation: A client wants to control a motorized projection screen and a legacy DVD player from a touch panel.
scenarios.notice: The screen requires a relay (momentary contact for up/down motors). The DVD player has no serial or IP control port.
scenarios.nextStep: Specify: relay module for screen control (up/down/stop using momentary contacts), IR emitter for DVD player control (attach to IR sensor on player). Both connected to the control processor.
scenarios.whyMatters: CTS-D designers must match control protocols to device capabilities. Not every device supports IP or serial control — relays and IR fill the gaps.

lessons.examRelevance: Control system design is part of Duty C (Task C1). Expect questions about protocol selection, user interface principles, and control architecture tiers. Know when to use RS-232 vs. IR vs. IP, and what relay contacts are used for.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which control protocol provides two-way communication and device status feedback over the network?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: IP control enables bidirectional communication — send commands AND query device status. IR is one-way. RS-232 is bidirectional but point-to-point wired. Relays are simple switches.

knowledgeCheck.question: What type of control output is used for a motorized projection screen?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Motorized screens use momentary relay contacts for up, down, and stop functions. The relay controls the motor circuit.

memorize: RS-232 = serial point-to-point, IR = one-way line-of-sight, IP = bidirectional network, Relay = physical switch
Control tiers: no control → keypad → full touch panel → enterprise networked
understand: Why simple user interfaces improve system adoption
When IR is the only option vs. a design compromise
practice: Specify the control protocol for each device in a 10-device conference room
examTraps: IR is one-way — you cannot confirm a device executed a command
RS-232 maximum distance is ~15m without an extender — use IP control for longer distances

lessons.summary: Control system design ranges from no-control huddle rooms to enterprise-networked campuses. Protocol selection depends on device capabilities: IP for modern devices (bidirectional), RS-232 for displays/projectors (reliable), IR for legacy devices (last resort), and relays for motorized equipment. User interfaces should be simple — 'Start Meeting' and 'End Meeting' cover 80% of use cases.

lessons.title: Networking for AV: VLANs, QoS, and AV-over-IP
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.domainAlignment: Duty B Task B4 + Duty C (combined ~15%)
lessons.overview: Design AV network infrastructure including VLAN segmentation, Quality of Service (QoS) policies, multicast management, and AV-over-IP architectures. Understand how AV traffic coexists with IT data on converged networks.
learningObjectives: Design VLAN architectures for AV traffic separation
Configure QoS priorities for real-time audio and video traffic
Understand multicast vs. unicast for AV distribution
Calculate bandwidth requirements for Dante, AES67, and video streaming
