Coordinate AV network requirements with IT security policies

keyTerms.definition: Switch feature that restricts multicast traffic to only ports with receivers that have requested the stream. Essential for AV-over-IP to prevent network flooding.
Differentiated Services Code Point — a field in the IP header used to classify and prioritize network traffic. Audio typically uses EF (46), video uses AF41 (34).
Digital Audio Network Through Ethernet — a standard for transmitting uncompressed, multi-channel audio over standard Ethernet with very low latency (<1ms).
An open standard for audio-over-IP interoperability. Enables cross-vendor audio networking. Dante devices can be AES67-compatible.
Power over Ethernet. PoE (802.3af): 15.4W. PoE+ (802.3at): 30W. PoE++ (802.3bt): 60-100W. Powers cameras, touch panels, ceiling mics, and small endpoints.
Ethernet frames larger than 1500 bytes (up to 9000 bytes). Used by some AV-over-IP systems to improve throughput efficiency.

lessons.content:
AV NETWORK DESIGN PRINCIPLES

Modern AV systems are network devices. The CTS-D designer must understand networking fundamentals to design systems that integrate with IT infrastructure.

VLAN ARCHITECTURE

Recommended VLAN separation:
- AV Control VLAN: Touch panels, control processors, DSPs, managed AV switches
- AV Media VLAN: Video encoders/decoders, Dante audio devices, streaming endpoints
- Corporate Data VLAN: Standard IT traffic (kept separate from AV)
- Management VLAN: Network switch management, monitoring tools

Why separate VLANs?
1. Multicast containment — AV multicast traffic won't flood data network
2. Security — AV devices isolated from corporate data
3. QoS — easier to apply traffic prioritization by VLAN
4. Troubleshooting — isolate AV network issues from data network issues

QUALITY OF SERVICE (QoS)

Priority levels for AV traffic:
1. Highest: Real-time audio (Dante, AES67) — DSCP EF (46) — latency-sensitive, loss-intolerant
2. High: Real-time video (conferencing, AV-over-IP) — DSCP AF41 (34) — latency-sensitive
3. Medium: Control traffic (touch panels, AMX/Crestron) — DSCP AF21 (18) — less latency-sensitive
4. Default: Best effort — all other traffic

Without QoS, a large file transfer can starve audio streams, causing dropouts.

MULTICAST FOR AV

Multicast allows one source to stream to multiple receivers simultaneously without duplicating traffic:
- AV-over-IP video distribution relies on multicast
- Dante audio uses multicast for subscriptions
- IGMP snooping MUST be enabled on all switches — without it, multicast floods every port
- IGMP querier must be configured (usually on a router or L3 switch)

BANDWIDTH REQUIREMENTS

Audio:
- Dante (48kHz/24-bit/stereo): ~2 Mbps per stereo channel
- Dante supports 512 channels on a 1GbE link
- AES67: similar bandwidth to Dante

Video:
- Compressed 1080p (H.264): 5-20 Mbps
- Compressed 4K (H.265): 15-50 Mbps
- Visually lossless 4K: 100-500 Mbps
- Uncompressed 4K (SDVoE): ~9 Gbps — requires 10GbE

POWER OVER ETHERNET (PoE)

PoE budget planning:
- List all PoE-powered AV devices (touch panels, cameras, ceiling mics, endpoints)
- Sum total wattage requirements
- Verify switch PoE budget exceeds total with 20% headroom
- Consider PoE class and whether PoE+ or PoE++ is needed for specific devices (PTZ cameras often need PoE+)

scenarios.situation: A Dante audio system has intermittent dropouts. IT reports no network issues on their monitoring dashboard.
scenarios.notice: IT monitoring typically doesn't look at AV VLANs or QoS markings. Standard monitoring may not detect short-duration packet loss that causes audio glitches.
scenarios.nextStep: Verify QoS is configured end-to-end (every switch in the path), IGMP snooping is enabled, Dante traffic is on a dedicated VLAN with EF marking, and no bandwidth bottlenecks exist on inter-switch links.
scenarios.whyMatters: Audio requires <1ms jitter and near-zero packet loss. Problems invisible to IT's general monitoring can be catastrophic for real-time audio.

lessons.examRelevance: Networking for AV spans both Duty B (IT coordination, Task B4 at 4%) and Duty C (system design). Expect questions about VLAN design, QoS DSCP values, multicast/IGMP, and bandwidth calculations for various AV-over-IP scenarios.

knowledgeCheck.question: What DSCP value should be assigned to real-time Dante audio traffic?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Expedited Forwarding (DSCP 46) provides the highest priority with minimal jitter and loss — required for real-time audio like Dante.

knowledgeCheck.question: What must be enabled on network switches to prevent multicast traffic from flooding all ports?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: IGMP snooping allows switches to learn which ports have multicast receivers and forward multicast only to those ports, preventing network flooding.

memorize: DSCP values: Audio EF(46), Video AF41(34), Control AF21(18)
IGMP snooping = required for multicast AV
understand: Why AV and IT traffic should be on separate VLANs
How QoS prevents data traffic from disrupting real-time audio/video
practice: Design a VLAN architecture for a 10-room AV-over-IP deployment
examTraps: Without IGMP snooping, multicast becomes broadcast and will saturate the network
QoS must be configured on EVERY switch in the path — a single switch without QoS breaks the chain

lessons.summary: AV network design requires VLAN separation (control, media, data), QoS prioritization (audio EF, video AF41), and IGMP snooping for multicast management. Dante/AES67 audio needs near-zero latency and packet loss. PoE budgets must account for all powered AV devices. Always coordinate VLAN and QoS requirements with IT before deployment.

lessons.title: Streaming, Security & AVIXA Standards Deep Dive
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Cover streaming architecture design for content distribution, security best practices for networked AV systems, and a comprehensive review of all AVIXA/ANSI standards referenced on the CTS-D exam.
learningObjectives: Design streaming architectures for live content distribution
Implement security best practices for networked AV systems
Identify and apply all AVIXA standards relevant to the CTS-D exam
Understand compression standards and their trade-offs
Specify secure remote access for AV system management

keyTerms.definition: Widely supported video compression standard. Good compression ratio. 1080p@60 typically 5-15 Mbps. Used in most streaming and conferencing.
Next-generation compression, ~50% more efficient than H.264. 4K@60 at 15-50 Mbps. Higher encoding compute requirements.
Network Device Interface — a software-based video-over-IP standard using compression for production-quality video over standard 1GbE networks.
Real Time Streaming Protocol — used for establishing and controlling streaming sessions between endpoints.
Display Image Size for 2D Content (DISCAS) — the standard defining minimum display sizes based on viewing distance and content type.
Rack Design for AV Systems — specifies rack layout, ventilation, cable management, and serviceability requirements.

lessons.content:
STREAMING ARCHITECTURE

Streaming Categories:

1. Internal Distribution: AV content distributed within a building or campus
- Encoders at sources, decoders at displays
- Managed via control system
- Low latency required for interactive use (<100ms)

2. External/Web Streaming: Content distributed to remote viewers
- Encoding to cloud platform (Teams, Zoom, YouTube, Vimeo)
- Higher latency acceptable (2-30 seconds)
- Bandwidth optimization critical
- CDN (Content Delivery Network) for large audiences

3. Recording/Archival: Content captured for later playback
- Recording server or cloud recording
- Metadata tagging for searchability
- Storage planning based on resolution and duration

COMPRESSION STANDARDS

H.264 (AVC):
- Most widely supported codec
- Good quality at moderate bandwidth
- Hardware encoders/decoders widely available
- Typical bitrates: 1080p = 5-15 Mbps, 4K = 20-40 Mbps

H.265 (HEVC):
- 50% more efficient than H.264
- Better quality at same bitrate or same quality at half bitrate
- Higher compute for encoding
- Typical bitrates: 1080p = 3-8 Mbps, 4K = 10-25 Mbps

AV1:
- Royalty-free alternative to HEVC
- Similar efficiency to HEVC
- Growing adoption in web/cloud streaming

SECURITY FOR NETWORKED AV

AV systems are network endpoints — they must follow security best practices:

1. Authentication:
- Change all default passwords on AV devices
- Use unique credentials per device or device class
- Implement 802.1X port authentication where supported

2. Network Security:
- VLAN isolation for AV traffic
- Firewall rules restricting AV device communication
- Disable unused ports and services on AV devices
- Use encrypted protocols (HTTPS, SSH) for management

3. Firmware Management:
- Maintain firmware update schedule
- Test updates in staging before production deployment
- Document firmware versions for all devices

4. Physical Security:
- Secure equipment rooms and racks
- Lock AV closets and network switches
- Tamper-resistant mounting for accessible devices

AVIXA STANDARDS REFERENCE

Key standards for CTS-D exam:

- V202.01 (DISCAS): Display image sizing — 4H/6H/8H rules
- V201.01: Image system contrast ratio (must account for ambient light)
- A102.01: Audio coverage uniformity — SPL variation across audience area
- A103.01: Spectral balance — frequency response consistency
- A104.01: Dynamic range in AV systems
- D401.01: Documentation requirements for AV systems
- D402.02: AV systems performance verification
- F501.01: Cable labeling standards
- F502.02: Rack design — ventilation, cable management, serviceability
- S601.01: Energy management for AV systems
lessons.examRelevance: Streaming design, security, and AVIXA standards are tested across Duty C. The standards are frequently referenced in exam questions — know what each standard covers, not necessarily the specific numbers within them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which AVIXA standard defines minimum display image size based on viewing distance?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: DISCAS (V202.01) is the Display Image Size for 2D Content standard, defining the 4H/6H/8H viewing distance rules.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which compression standard offers approximately 50% better efficiency than H.264?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: H.265 (HEVC) achieves approximately the same quality as H.264 at half the bitrate, or significantly better quality at the same bitrate.

memorize: AVIXA standards: V202.01=display sizing, V201.01=contrast, A102.01=coverage, D401.01=documentation, F502.02=racks
H.265 = ~50% more efficient than H.264
Default passwords = #1 AV security vulnerability
understand: Why AV devices are network security risks if not properly secured
The difference between internal low-latency distribution and external web streaming
practice: Match each AVIXA standard number to its purpose from memory
examTraps: V202.01 (DISCAS) is about image SIZE — V201.01 is about CONTRAST RATIO — don't confuse them
Security questions on the exam often test awareness of basic practices, not deep cybersecurity knowledge

lessons.summary: Streaming architecture depends on use case: internal (low latency), external (CDN-based), or recording. H.265 offers 50% efficiency gain over H.264. AV security follows IT best practices: change defaults, VLAN isolation, firmware management. Know all AVIXA standards by number and purpose — V202.01 (display size), V201.01 (contrast), A102.01 (audio coverage), D401.01 (documentation), F502.02 (rack design).

lessons.title: Signal Flow Diagrams & System Block Diagrams
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Create professional signal flow diagrams and system block diagrams that clearly communicate AV system architecture. These are the most important technical drawings in the AV design package.
learningObjectives: Create signal flow diagrams showing audio, video, and control signal paths
Design system block diagrams that communicate system architecture to integrators
Use standard symbols and conventions for AV drawings
Distinguish between functional block diagrams and detailed signal flow diagrams
Document input/output connections, signal types, and connector specifications

keyTerms.definition: A drawing showing the path of audio, video, and control signals through an AV system, including every device, connection type, and signal format.
A high-level drawing showing major system components and their relationships without detailed connection information. Used for design review and client communication.
A simplified signal flow showing one line per signal path instead of individual conductors. Shows system architecture at a glance.
A detailed table listing every input and output connection on each device: port number, signal type, cable type, destination, and label.
A key on the drawing defining all symbols, line types, abbreviations, and conventions used.

lessons.content:
SIGNAL FLOW DIAGRAMS — THE CORE AV DESIGN DOCUMENT

The signal flow diagram is the most critical technical document in an AV design package. It shows every signal path through the system — how audio, video, control, and network signals flow from sources through processing to destinations.

SIGNAL FLOW COMPONENTS

1. Sources (left side of diagram):
- Laptop inputs (HDMI, USB-C)
- Wireless presentation devices
- Camera feeds
- Microphone inputs
- Media players
- Document cameras

2. Processing (center):
- Video switchers / matrix
- DSP (audio processor)
- Control processor
- Network switches
- Scalers / converters

3. Destinations (right side):
- Displays / projectors
- Speakers / amplifiers
- Recording devices
- Streaming encoders
- Far-end video codec output

DRAWING CONVENTIONS

Line types for signal types:
- Solid line: Video signal
- Dashed line: Audio signal
- Dotted line: Control signal
- Double line: Network/data
- Line color coding may also be used (blue=video, red=audio, green=control)

Each line should indicate:
- Signal format (HDMI, HDBaseT, Cat6, RS-232, etc.)
- Cable type if non-obvious
- Connector type at each end
- Direction of signal flow (arrow)

SYSTEM BLOCK DIAGRAMS

Simplified version of signal flow for non-technical stakeholders:
- Show major functional blocks (not individual devices)
- Example blocks: 'Presentation Sources,' 'Video Distribution,' 'Display System,' 'Audio System,' 'Control'
- Show relationships between blocks
- Used during SD and client presentations
- Detail increases through DD and CD phases

BEST PRACTICES

1. Signal flows read left to right (source → destination)
2. Group related signals: audio paths together, video paths together
3. Label every connection with signal type and cable type
4. Include device model numbers on CD-phase drawings
5. Create a legend defining all symbols and line types
6. Include I/O schedules cross-referencing the signal flow
7. Number every device consistently with equipment schedule
8. Show power connections to critical equipment

scenarios.situation: An integrator submits a shop drawing that shows a DSP connected directly to speakers without an amplifier.
scenarios.notice: DSPs output line-level audio — they cannot drive speakers directly. An amplifier is required.
scenarios.nextStep: Return the shop drawing marked 'Revise and Resubmit' with a note indicating an amplifier is required between the DSP output and speakers. Reference the original signal flow diagram showing the amplifier in the audio chain.
scenarios.whyMatters: Shop drawing review is a core CTS-D responsibility. Catching errors before installation prevents costly rework.

lessons.examRelevance: Signal flow diagrams and system documentation are core Duty C topics (Tasks C1 and C3). Expect questions about proper signal flow conventions, what information must appear on drawings, and how to interpret signal paths.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a standard signal flow diagram, which direction do signals flow?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AV signal flow convention: sources on the left, processing in the center, destinations on the right. Signals flow left to right.

knowledgeCheck.question: What document cross-references every physical connection shown in a signal flow diagram?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The cable/I/O schedule lists every connection: source device port, cable type and number, destination device port. It's the detailed companion to the signal flow diagram.

memorize: Signal flow: left to right, sources → processing → destinations
Line types: solid=video, dashed=audio, dotted=control
Every connection must show: signal format, cable type, direction
understand: The difference between a system block diagram (high-level) and signal flow diagram (detailed)
Why signal flows are the most important technical document for integrators
practice: Draw a signal flow for a standard conference room with video conferencing
examTraps: A system block diagram is NOT a signal flow — it's a simplified overview
Signal flow diagrams at CD phase must include specific equipment model numbers

lessons.summary: Signal flow diagrams are the core AV design document, showing every audio, video, and control signal path from source to destination. They flow left to right with standard line conventions. System block diagrams provide a simplified overview for non-technical stakeholders. Both are essential Duty C deliverables — signal flows become increasingly detailed from SD through CD phases.

lessons.title: Equipment Schedules, Cable Schedules & Bill of Materials
lessons.module: Day 2: Core AV Design — Video, Audio, Acoustics & Networking
lessons.overview: Create comprehensive project documentation including equipment schedules, cable schedules, and bills of materials. These documents are essential for accurate bidding, procurement, and installation.
learningObjectives: Create equipment schedules with proper labeling and specification references
Design cable schedules that map every connection in the system
Build accurate Bills of Materials (BOMs) for procurement
Apply AVIXA F501.01 cable labeling standards
Understand CSI MasterFormat for AV specifications

keyTerms.definition: A table listing every AV device: item number, manufacturer, model, description, quantity, location, and specification reference.
A table listing every cable: cable number, type, source device/port, destination device/port, length, and label.
A comprehensive list of all materials needed for the project: equipment, cables, connectors, mounting hardware, and accessories with quantities and part numbers.
Construction Specifications Institute's standard organization for construction specifications. AV falls under Division 27 (Communications) or Division 11 (Equipment).
Cable labeling standard defining consistent, readable labels at both ends of every AV cable for maintenance and troubleshooting.

lessons.content:
EQUIPMENT SCHEDULES

An equipment schedule catalogs every AV device in the project:

Columns:
- Item Number: Unique identifier (e.g., V-01, A-01, C-01 for video, audio, control)
- Manufacturer: Brand name
- Model Number: Exact model
- Description: What it does
- Quantity: How many
- Location: Room or area designation
- Specification Section: CSI reference
- Notes: Special requirements (requires PoE, ceiling mount, etc.)

Naming conventions:
- V-xx: Video devices (displays, projectors, cameras, encoders)
- A-xx: Audio devices (microphones, speakers, amplifiers, DSP)
- C-xx: Control devices (processors, touch panels, keypads)
- N-xx: Network devices (switches, wireless APs)
- P-xx: Power devices (UPS, power sequencer)

CABLE SCHEDULES

Every cable in the system must be documented:

Columns:
- Cable Number: Unique label matching physical cable label
- Cable Type: Cat6A, HDMI, XLR, coax, fiber, etc.
- Source Device: Item number + specific port
- Destination Device: Item number + specific port
- Length: Estimated cable run length
- Conduit/Pathway: Which conduit or pathway carries this cable
- Notes: Plenum-rated, shielded, etc.

AVIXA F501.01 Cable Labeling:
- Labels at BOTH ends of every cable
- Label includes: Cable number, source, destination
- Machine-printed labels (no handwriting)
- Labels must be durable and legible in the installed environment

BILL OF MATERIALS (BOM)

The BOM is used for procurement and cost estimation:
- All equipment from the equipment schedule
- All cables with lengths and connectors
- All mounting hardware (brackets, adapters, plates)
- All accessories (remotes, tools, spare parts)
- Rack accessories (shelves, panels, power strips)
- Infrastructure items (wall plates, floor boxes, conduit fittings)

CSI MASTERFORMAT FOR AV

AV specifications are typically written in CSI format:
- Division 27: Communications (preferred for AV in most specifications)
  - Section 27 41 00: Audio-Video Systems
  - Section 27 41 16: Integrated Audio-Video Systems and Equipment
- Division 11: Equipment (used when AV is categorized as specialty equipment)

Specification sections typically include:
- Part 1: General (scope, submittals, quality assurance)
- Part 2: Products (equipment specifications, standards compliance)
- Part 3: Execution (installation, testing, training, closeout)
lessons.examRelevance: Task C4 (Finalize project documentation) is worth 10% of the CTS-D exam. Expect questions about what belongs in equipment schedules vs. cable schedules, proper cable labeling per AVIXA F501.01, and CSI MasterFormat organization.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to AVIXA F501.01, cable labels must be placed:
options: At both ends of every cable
Only on cables longer than 10 feet
knowledgeCheck.answer: At both ends of every cable
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AVIXA F501.01 requires machine-printed, durable labels at both ends of every AV cable for easy identification during installation and maintenance.

knowledgeCheck.question: In CSI MasterFormat, AV systems are most commonly specified under which division?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Division 27 (Communications) is the standard location for AV specifications in CSI MasterFormat.

memorize: Equipment prefixes: V=video, A=audio, C=control, N=network, P=power
F501.01: labels at BOTH ends, machine-printed, durable
CSI Division 27 = Communications (AV home)
understand: Why cable schedules must cross-reference signal flow diagrams
How BOMs differ from equipment schedules (BOMs include ALL materials, not just equipment)
practice: Create an equipment schedule for a standard conference room
examTraps: A BOM includes cables, connectors, mounting hardware, and accessories — not just major equipment
CSI Division 27, not Division 16 (which was the old electrical division)

lessons.summary: Project documentation includes equipment schedules (every device with model/quantity/location), cable schedules (every connection with cable type/routing), and BOMs (all materials for procurement). AVIXA F501.01 requires machine-printed labels at both cable ends. AV specifications use CSI MasterFormat Division 27. These documents are essential for accurate bidding and quality installation.

lessons.title: Rack Design & Infrastructure Documentation
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Design AV equipment racks following AVIXA F502.02 standards, create rack elevation drawings, and document all infrastructure requirements including conduit, power, and cooling for AV systems.
learningObjectives: Design rack layouts following AVIXA F502.02 rack design standard
Create rack elevation drawings showing front and rear views
Calculate rack space requirements using standard rack unit (RU) measurements
Plan ventilation, cable management, and serviceability in rack designs
Document conduit pathways, power requirements, and cooling for equipment rooms

keyTerms.definition: Standard measurement for rack-mounted equipment: 1 RU = 1.75 inches (44.45mm). A standard full-height rack is 42 RU.
Rack Design for AV Systems standard — specifies ventilation, cable management, serviceability, and organization requirements.
A front and/or rear view drawing of equipment mounted in a rack, showing exact placement of each device by RU position.
Organized routing of cables within and between racks using vertical and horizontal cable managers, service loops, and labeling.
An arrangement where equipment intake faces one direction (cold aisle) and exhaust faces the other (hot aisle) for efficient cooling.
The number of rack units a piece of equipment occupies. A 2U device takes up 3.5 inches of rack space.

lessons.content:
RACK DESIGN FUNDAMENTALS

Standard rack dimensions:
- Width: 19 inches (standard EIA/ECA-310)
- Height: 42 RU (73.5 inches) is standard full-height
- Depth: 24-42 inches (deeper racks for servers, 24-30" typical for AV)
- 1 RU = 1.75 inches

RACK LAYOUT BEST PRACTICES (AVIXA F502.02)

1. Equipment Organization (top to bottom):
- Top: Lightweight equipment, patch panels
- Middle: Heavy equipment (amplifiers, power supplies)
- Bottom: Heaviest items for stability

2. Ventilation:
- Blanking panels on all unused RU spaces (prevents hot air recirculation)
- Minimum 1 RU spacer between heat-generating devices
- Fan trays or active ventilation for sealed racks
- Maintain front-to-back airflow
- Maximum recommended rack temperature: 95°F (35°C)

3. Cable Management:
- Vertical cable managers on both sides of the rack
- Horizontal cable managers between major sections
- Service loops at patch panels for easy re-termination
- Cable routing: power cables on one side, signal cables on the other
- Label all cables per AVIXA F501.01

4. Serviceability:
- All devices must be accessible for maintenance without removing other devices
- Sliding shelves for equipment requiring top access
- Rear access required — never install racks flush against a wall
- Minimum 36 inches clearance in front, 24 inches in rear
- Document rack layout with elevation drawings

5. Power:
- Dedicated circuits per rack (or per rack row)
- Power distribution units (PDUs) mounted vertically in rack
- Separate PDUs for critical vs. non-critical equipment
- UPS for control processors and network equipment

RACK ELEVATION DRAWINGS

A rack elevation shows:
- Front view: Every device in its RU position
- Rear view: Cable connections, PDU placement
- Labels: Device name, model, item number (matching equipment schedule)
- RU numbers marked on the side
- Power connections indicated
- Network connections indicated

INFRASTRUCTURE DOCUMENTATION

The AV design package includes:
- Floor plans showing equipment locations, floor boxes, wall plates
- RCP showing ceiling-mounted devices
- Conduit pathway drawings (size and routing)
- Power plan showing circuit assignments
- Rack elevation drawings
- Cable schedule with pathway assignments
lessons.examRelevance: Rack design (F502.02) and infrastructure documentation are tested in Duty C Tasks C3 and C4, which combined are worth 20% of the exam. Expect questions about rack organization, ventilation requirements, serviceability clearances, and rack elevation drawing conventions.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to AVIXA F502.02, what should fill unused rack spaces?
options: Nothing — leave them open for airflow
Blanking panels to prevent hot air recirculation
knowledgeCheck.answer: Blanking panels to prevent hot air recirculation
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Open rack spaces allow hot exhaust air to recirculate to equipment intakes. Blanking panels maintain proper front-to-back airflow.

knowledgeCheck.question: How many inches does a 2 RU device occupy in a standard rack?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 1 RU = 1.75 inches. A 2 RU device = 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 inches.

memorize: 1 RU = 1.75 inches, standard rack = 42 RU
Rack clearance: 36" front, 24" rear minimum
Heavy equipment at bottom, light at top
Blanking panels on all unused spaces
understand: Why ventilation design is critical — rack overheating is a top reliability issue
Why rear access is mandatory and racks should never be against a wall
practice: Design a rack layout for a 10-device AV system
examTraps: Don't forget blanking panels — open spaces cause overheating, not cooling
Rack depth matters — AV racks are typically 24-30" deep, shorter than server racks

lessons.summary: Rack design follows AVIXA F502.02: heavy equipment at bottom, blanking panels on empty spaces, 36" front / 24" rear clearance, and proper cable management. 1 RU = 1.75 inches. Rack elevation drawings show exact device placement with matching equipment schedule item numbers. Infrastructure documentation includes floor plans, RCPs, conduit drawings, and power plans.

lessons.title: AV Floor Plans, Elevations & Reflected Ceiling Plans
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Create AV-specific construction drawings including floor plans with equipment locations, wall elevations showing mounting details, and reflected ceiling plans for overhead equipment placement.
learningObjectives: Add AV device locations to architectural floor plans
Create wall elevations showing display heights, control panel locations, and camera positions
Document speaker, projector, and microphone locations on reflected ceiling plans
Apply proper AV drawing symbols and annotations
Coordinate AV drawings with the architectural drawing set

keyTerms.definition: Above Finished Floor — the standard reference for mounting heights. Example: 'Display center at 60" AFF.'
A standardized set of symbols used on AV drawings to represent equipment: speakers, microphones, displays, cameras, projectors, floor boxes, etc.
An enlarged view of a specific construction element showing exact dimensions, materials, and assembly instructions for the installer.
Text labels on drawings that identify equipment, reference specifications, provide mounting instructions, and note special requirements.
A combined drawing showing multiple disciplines' work in the same space to identify conflicts before construction.

lessons.content:
AV FLOOR PLANS

AV floor plans overlay equipment locations on the architect's base floor plan:

Equipment shown on floor plans:
- Display locations (wall-mounted, floor-standing, or ceiling-mounted)
- Floor boxes (power, data, AV connections)
- Wall plates (input plates, output plates)
- Equipment racks and credenzas
- Camera positions (wall or ceiling mounted)
- Table-mounted devices (microphones, connection panels)
- Assistive listening transmitter location

Key information:
- Equipment item number (from equipment schedule)
- Mounting type (W = wall, C = ceiling, F = floor, T = table)
- Reference to detail drawing for mounting specifics
- Conduit paths between equipment locations

WALL ELEVATIONS

Elevations show the vertical layout of wall-mounted equipment:

Critical dimensions:
- Display center height: Typically 60" AFF for seated viewing, 66-72" AFF for standing/mixed
- Touch panel height: 42-48" AFF center (ADA accessible range is 15-48" AFF)
- Camera height: Above or beside display, typically 66-72" AFF
- Microphone height (wall mount): 72-84" AFF
- Floor box locations shown in plan, referenced from elevation

Elevation components:
- Display outline with dimensions
- Wall plate locations with device schedule reference
- Conduit entry points (typically from above or below)
- Blocking/backing requirements noted
- ADA reach range compliance indicated

REFLECTED CEILING PLANS (RCP)

AV devices on the RCP:
- Ceiling speakers (symbol + item number)
- Projectors (with throw line to screen)
- Ceiling microphones (with coverage area indication)
- PTZ cameras (with field of view indication)
- Ceiling-mounted displays (with support structure)

RCP coordination:
- Verify no conflicts with light fixtures, HVAC diffusers, fire sprinklers
- Maintain minimum distances between speakers and microphones
- Confirm ceiling grid module alignment for in-ceiling devices
- Note ceiling construction type and height

DRAWING COORDINATION

AV drawings must be coordinated with:
- Architectural: Room layout, wall construction, ceiling type
- Electrical: Power outlet locations, dedicated circuits
- Mechanical: HVAC diffuser locations (noise, airflow on microphones)
- IT/Telecom: Network drop locations
- Structural: Blocking for heavy displays, ceiling structure for projectors
- Lighting: Fixture locations affecting display visibility

scenarios.situation: On the RCP, a ceiling speaker is shown directly adjacent to an HVAC return air diffuser.
scenarios.notice: The diffuser will create airflow noise directly next to the speaker, and the opening may prevent proper speaker mounting.
scenarios.nextStep: Relocate the speaker at least 3 feet from the diffuser, maintaining coverage requirements. Issue a revised RCP and coordinate the change with the mechanical engineer.
scenarios.whyMatters: HVAC diffuser noise can significantly impact speaker performance and intelligibility. CTS-D designers must review RCPs for conflicts with mechanical elements.

lessons.examRelevance: AV construction drawings are core Duty C deliverables (Task C3, 10% of exam). Expect questions about what appears on floor plans vs. RCPs vs. elevations, proper mounting heights, and drawing coordination between disciplines.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the standard reference for AV equipment mounting heights on elevation drawings?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AFF (Above Finished Floor) is the standard reference for all mounting height dimensions on AV elevation drawings.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which drawing type should show the location of ceiling speakers relative to HVAC diffusers?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The RCP shows all ceiling elements including speakers, diffusers, lights, and sprinklers — enabling coordination between disciplines.

memorize: Display center: 60" AFF seated, 66-72" AFF standing
Touch panel: 42-48" AFF (ADA range 15-48")
Floor plans = horizontal devices, RCP = ceiling devices, Elevations = wall-mounted devices
understand: Why coordination between AV and mechanical (HVAC) on the RCP is critical
How AFF dimensions ensure consistent installation across rooms
practice: Mark up an architectural floor plan with AV equipment locations for a conference room
examTraps: Elevations show HEIGHT, floor plans show LOCATION — don't confuse which information belongs on which drawing
ADA reach range (15-48" AFF) applies to touch panels and controls — not displays

lessons.summary: AV construction drawings include floor plans (device locations), wall elevations (mounting heights in AFF), and RCPs (ceiling-mounted equipment). Key heights: displays at 60" AFF seated, touch panels at 42-48" AFF (ADA compliant). RCP coordination with HVAC, lighting, and fire sprinklers prevents construction conflicts. All drawings must reference the equipment schedule and include proper AV symbols.

lessons.title: Electrical Infrastructure & Power Design
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Design electrical infrastructure for AV systems including power distribution, circuit sizing, grounding, UPS systems, and the critical coordination required with electrical engineers during the design process.
learningObjectives: Calculate total AV power requirements including headroom and derating
Specify circuit types: dedicated, isolated ground, UPS-backed
Design power distribution for equipment racks and remote devices
Understand grounding and bonding requirements for AV systems
Create power schedules and coordinate with electrical engineers

keyTerms.definition: A dedicated ground conductor that runs directly back to the electrical panel without connection to other grounds. Reduces electrical noise in sensitive audio systems.
A device that powers equipment on/off in a specific order to prevent transient damage. Amplifiers should power on last and off first.
Power Distribution Unit — a rack-mounted device that distributes power to multiple devices from a single circuit, often with monitoring and switching capabilities.
Uninterruptible Power Supply — provides battery backup power during outages. Critical for control processors and network equipment to prevent data loss and enable graceful shutdown.
The brief surge of current when equipment powers on, which can be 5-10× the steady-state current. Affects circuit breaker selection.

lessons.content:
AV POWER DESIGN

Power design is a coordination exercise between the CTS-D designer and the electrical engineer. The AV designer specifies requirements; the electrical engineer implements them.

CIRCUIT SIZING REVIEW

Standard North American power:
- 120V / 15A circuit: 1,800W total, 1,440W usable (80% continuous derating)
- 120V / 20A circuit: 2,400W total, 1,920W usable
- 208V / 20A circuit: 4,160W total, 3,328W usable (for heavy loads)

NEC 80% rule: For continuous loads (running 3+ hours — which covers most AV), circuit loading must not exceed 80% of the breaker rating.

POWER SCHEDULE

Create a power schedule listing:
- Circuit designation (AV-1, AV-2, etc.)
- Voltage and amperage
- Type: standard, dedicated, isolated ground, UPS
- Location: rack, wall outlet, floor box, ceiling
- Devices served (reference equipment schedule)
- Total load (watts and amps)
- Notes: power sequencer, time delay, emergency power

POWER DISTRIBUTION STRATEGIES

1. Equipment Rack:
- Minimum: One dedicated 20A circuit per rack
- Recommended: Two circuits per rack (redundancy, load distribution)
- PDU(s) mounted vertically in rack
- Separate circuits for amplifiers (high current) and processors (clean power)

2. Display Locations:
- Dedicated circuit at each display location
- Outlet behind display (recessed box for flat mount)
- 20A circuit for large displays (98"+) due to inrush current

3. Floor Boxes:
- Power + data in floor boxes at conference tables
- Coordinate location with furniture layout
- Must be accessible and code-compliant

4. Ceiling Locations:
- Projector: dedicated circuit at ceiling mount point
- Other ceiling devices: verify PoE capability to avoid ceiling power needs

GROUNDING

- All AV equipment must be properly grounded
- Audio systems benefit from isolated ground circuits
- Never lift ground pins — this is a safety code violation
- Ground loops cause audible hum — isolated grounds and balanced audio connections prevent them
- For sensitive audio: star grounding topology (all grounds terminate at a single point)

UPS REQUIREMENTS

- Control processors: UPS for clean shutdown and instant recovery
- Network switches: UPS to maintain network during power blips
- DSP: UPS if conference calls must survive brief outages
- Displays/projectors: Generally NO UPS (high power draw, acceptable to restart)
- Size UPS for runtime needed: typically 10-15 minutes for graceful shutdown

workedExamples.given: AV rack contains: 2 amplifiers (400W each), 1 DSP (75W), 1 control processor (50W), 1 network switch (120W), and 3 HDBaseT receivers (15W each).
workedExamples.solution:
Total load = 800 + 75 + 50 + 120 + 45 = 1,090W
Usable per 20A circuit = 2,400 × 0.8 = 1,920W
1,090W < 1,920W — fits on one circuit.
However, best practice separates amplifiers (high current, noisy) from processors (clean power).
Circuit 1: Amplifiers = 800W
Circuit 2: Processors + network = 290W (with UPS)
workedExamples.answer: Technically 1 circuit sufficient, but best practice = 2 dedicated circuits (one for amplifiers, one UPS-backed for processors).
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Putting everything on one circuit works mathematically but amplifier inrush current can trip breakers and amplifier noise can affect DSP/control equipment.

lessons.examRelevance: Power infrastructure is tested in Duty C Tasks C2 and C4. Expect questions about circuit sizing (80% rule), isolated grounds, UPS requirements, and power distribution strategies. Math questions will involve power calculations.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the maximum continuous load for a 120V, 20A circuit per NEC?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 20A × 120V = 2,400W total capacity. NEC requires 80% derating for continuous loads: 2,400 × 0.8 = 1,920W.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which AV devices should be connected to a UPS?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: UPS protects critical low-power devices that need clean shutdown. Displays and amplifiers draw too much power and can restart safely.

memorize: 20A circuit = 1,920W usable (80% of 2,400W)
15A circuit = 1,440W usable (80% of 1,800W)
UPS for: control processors, network switches, DSP. NOT for: displays, amplifiers
understand: Why isolated grounds prevent audio system hum
Why amplifiers should be on separate circuits from sensitive processors
practice: Create a power schedule for a conference room AV system
examTraps: Never forget the 80% derating — 2,400W is the BREAKER rating, not the usable load
Never lift a ground pin — always solve ground loop problems properly with balanced connections and isolated grounds

lessons.summary: AV power design requires the 80% continuous load rule (20A = 1,920W usable), separate circuits for amplifiers and processors, UPS for critical low-power devices, and proper grounding. Create power schedules coordinated with electrical engineers. Isolated grounds reduce audio noise. Never lift ground pins — solve ground loops with balanced connections and proper grounding topology.

lessons.title: System Commissioning & Performance Verification
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Master the commissioning process: verifying installed AV systems against design specifications, conducting performance measurements using AVIXA verification standards, and ensuring systems meet functional requirements before client acceptance.
learningObjectives: Execute a systematic commissioning process from pre-testing through client acceptance
Apply AVIXA D402.02 performance verification procedures
Measure and verify audio system performance (SPL, coverage, frequency response, intelligibility)
Measure and verify video system performance (brightness, contrast, color, resolution)
Document commissioning results and create verification reports

keyTerms.definition: The systematic process of testing, adjusting, and verifying that an installed AV system meets design specifications and functional requirements.
AV Systems Performance Verification standard — defines procedures for measuring and documenting system performance against design criteria.
A broadband test signal with equal energy per octave, used for measuring room acoustics and speaker frequency response.
Measured in Kelvin (K), describes the white point of a display. 6500K (D65) is the standard for video production.
A formal document recording all commissioning measurements, pass/fail results, and any deviations from design specifications.

lessons.content:
THE COMMISSIONING PROCESS

Commissioning is the CTS-D designer's quality assurance checkpoint. It verifies the integrator built what was designed.

COMMISSIONING PHASES

1. Pre-Commissioning Review:
- Verify all equipment matches specification (correct models, firmware versions)
- Inspect physical installation quality (mounting, cable management, labeling)
- Verify cable labels match cable schedule
- Check rack layout against rack elevation drawings
- Verify power and network connectivity

2. Functional Testing:
- Power on/off sequences
- Source switching (every input to every output)
- Control system operation (every button/function)
- Audio routing and level verification
- Video routing and quality verification
- Network connectivity and device communication

3. Performance Verification (per AVIXA D402.02):

Audio Measurements:
- SPL levels: Measure at listener positions, verify adequate level (typically 70-80 dB SPL for speech)
- Coverage uniformity (A102.01): SPL variation across seating area should be ≤ ±3 dB
- Frequency response: Verify spectral balance per A103.01
- Speech intelligibility: STI/STIPA measurement ≥ 0.60 for 'good' rating
- Background noise: Verify NC rating meets specification
- Echo cancellation: Verify AEC performance during video calls

Video Measurements:
- Display brightness: Measure in actual room lighting conditions
- Contrast ratio: System contrast ratio including ambient light per V201.01
- Color accuracy: Check color temperature (target 6500K/D65)
- Resolution: Verify native resolution content displays at full resolution
- Image sizing: Verify display size meets DISCAS requirements per V202.01

Control Measurements:
- Response time: User action to system response
- Macro execution: All automated sequences operate correctly
- Scheduling: Room booking integration functions properly
- Remote management: Monitoring and control from NOC

4. Client Acceptance:
- Demonstrate system to client stakeholders
- Walk through all use cases identified in needs assessment
- Document any deficiencies on punch list
- Obtain formal acceptance signature

DOCUMENTATION

Verification report includes:
- Test procedures performed
- Measurement results with pass/fail
- Equipment verification (model/serial/firmware log)
- Photographs of completed installation
- Deviations from design and resolutions
- Punch list items (if any)
- Sign-off from designer, integrator, and client

scenarios.situation: During audio commissioning, SPL measurements show ±6 dB variation across the seating area in a training room.
scenarios.notice: AVIXA A102.01 specifies audio coverage uniformity of ±3 dB. The ±6 dB variation is out of spec.
scenarios.nextStep: Investigate causes: check speaker placement against design, verify DSP delay and EQ settings, measure individual speaker output levels. Adjust tap settings, re-aim speakers, or add/relocate speakers to achieve ±3 dB uniformity.
scenarios.whyMatters: Performance verification catches installation deviations from design intent. A ±6 dB variation means some seats hear speech twice as loud as others — unacceptable for a training room.

lessons.examRelevance: Tasks D1 and D2 combined represent 10% of the CTS-D exam. Expect questions about the commissioning process, AVIXA verification standards, acceptable measurement thresholds, and what should appear in a verification report.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the acceptable SPL variation across the audience area per AVIXA A102.01?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AVIXA A102.01 specifies ±3 dB maximum SPL variation for audio coverage uniformity. Greater variation means inconsistent listening experience.

knowledgeCheck.question: What color temperature should displays be calibrated to for standard video?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: D65 (6500K) is the international standard white point for video production and display calibration.

memorize: Audio coverage uniformity: ±3 dB (A102.01)
STI ≥ 0.60 for 'good' intelligibility
Display color temp: 6500K (D65)
Speech SPL target: 70-80 dB SPL at listener
understand: Why commissioning by the designer (not the integrator) provides quality assurance
How ambient light affects system contrast ratio measurements
practice: Create a commissioning checklist for a conference room
examTraps: Performance verification is done by or supervised by the DESIGNER, not the integrator alone
System contrast ratio (V201.01) is measured WITH ambient light, not in a dark room

lessons.summary: Commissioning verifies installed systems meet design specifications. Key thresholds: audio coverage ±3 dB (A102.01), STI ≥ 0.60, display color 6500K (D65). The process flows: pre-commissioning inspection → functional testing → performance verification (D402.02) → client acceptance. Document everything in a verification report with measurements, pass/fail results, and sign-offs.

lessons.title: Project Closeout: As-Builts, Training & Handoff
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Complete the project lifecycle with proper closeout procedures: as-built documentation, Operations & Maintenance manuals, end-user training, and formal project handoff to the client.
learningObjectives: Create as-built documentation reflecting actual installed conditions
Compile comprehensive Operations & Maintenance (O&M) manuals
Design end-user training programs for different user skill levels
Execute formal project handoff with warranty documentation
Manage punch list resolution and final acceptance

keyTerms.definition: Updated design drawings reflecting the actual installed conditions — every deviation from the original design documented.
Operations and Maintenance Manual — a comprehensive reference for operating and maintaining the installed AV system.
The manufacturer's and integrator's commitment to repair or replace defective equipment/workmanship within a defined period.
The point at which the system is sufficiently complete for the client to use it for its intended purpose, even if punch list items remain.
The formal client acknowledgment that the project is complete, all punch list items are resolved, and the warranty period begins.

lessons.content:
PROJECT CLOSEOUT

Closeout is the final phase of the AV project. It ensures the client has everything needed to operate, maintain, and eventually refresh the system.

AS-BUILT DOCUMENTATION

As-built drawings update the original design to reflect what was actually installed:
- Equipment locations that changed during construction
- Cable routing modifications
- Equipment substitutions (different model than specified)
- Additional devices added via change order
- IP addresses and network configuration
- Control system programming changes

As-built rule: If it's different from the design drawings, it must be documented.

O&M MANUAL CONTENTS

1. System Overview:
- Description of system functionality
- Signal flow diagrams (as-built)
- Equipment list with serial numbers and firmware versions

2. Operating Instructions:
- Step-by-step procedures for common tasks
- Screenshots of control system interfaces
- Troubleshooting guide (common issues and solutions)

3. Maintenance Schedule:
- Preventive maintenance tasks and intervals
- Filter cleaning schedule (projectors, equipment rooms)
- Lamp/laser replacement guidelines
- Firmware update procedures

4. Technical Reference:
- As-built drawings (signal flow, floor plans, rack elevations)
- Cable schedule
- Network configuration (IP addresses, VLANs, passwords)
- Equipment manuals (manufacturer PDFs)

5. Contact Information:
- Integrator support contacts
- Manufacturer support lines
- Warranty claim procedures

END-USER TRAINING

Training levels:
1. Operator Training (all users):
- How to start/end a meeting
- Source switching and volume control
- Video conferencing operation
- What to do when something goes wrong (who to call)

2. Administrator Training (IT/facilities staff):
- Control system programming access
- Network configuration and monitoring
- Equipment replacement procedures
- Firmware update process

3. Train-the-Trainer:
- Comprehensive training for designated staff who will train future users
- Includes documentation and reference materials

PUNCH LIST MANAGEMENT

The punch list is a list of deficiencies identified during final walkthrough:
- Each item: description, location, responsible party, due date
- Items classified: cosmetic, functional, or design deviation
- Resolution timeline agreed upon (typically 30 days)
- All items must be resolved before final acceptance and payment

WARRANTY AND HANDOFF

- Equipment warranty: typically 1-3 years from manufacturer
- Integrator workmanship warranty: typically 1 year
- Warranty start date: usually at substantial completion or final acceptance
- Document all warranty terms, claim procedures, and contact information
- Provide client with spare parts recommendations and replacement planning

lessons.title: Advanced AV Math: PAG/NAG, Display Sizing & Electrical Calculations
lessons.module: Day 3: Documentation, Deployment & Exam Mastery
lessons.overview: Practice advanced CTS-D exam math problems including complete PAG/NAG analysis for sound reinforcement, complex DISCAS display sizing with mixed content, multi-circuit electrical load calculations, and acoustic treatment analysis.
learningObjectives: Solve complete PAG/NAG problems with all variables
Calculate display sizes for complex rooms with multiple viewer zones
Perform multi-circuit electrical load analysis with thermal calculations
Apply the Sabine equation to determine if acoustic treatment is needed
Combine multiple formulas in real-world design scenarios

keyTerms.definition: Feedback Stability Margin — typically 6 dB of headroom subtracted from PAG to ensure stable operation without feedback.
The distance from a source where direct sound and reverberant sound are equal in level. Beyond Dc, intelligibility drops rapidly.
A value from 0 to 1 representing a surface's ability to absorb sound. 0 = perfectly reflective, 1 = perfectly absorptive.
The unit of sound absorption. One sabin equals the absorption of 1 square foot (or 1 square meter for metric sabins) of a perfectly absorptive surface.

lessons.content:
ADVANCED MATH PRACTICE

This lesson focuses on multi-step calculations that combine several formulas — the type of problems that appear on the CTS-D exam.

PAG/NAG COMPLETE ANALYSIS

The full PAG equation:
PAG = 20×log(D1) - 20×log(D2) + 20×log(D0) - 20×log(DS) - 10×log(NOM) - FSM

Where:
- D1 = Loudspeaker to farthest listener
- D2 = Loudspeaker to nearest open microphone
- D0 = Talker to nearest microphone
- DS = Talker to farthest listener (without system)
- NOM = Number of open microphones
- FSM = Feedback stability margin (6 dB standard)

NAG = 20×log(DS) - 20×log(D0)

Design check: PAG ≥ NAG means the system can provide enough gain without feedback.

COMPLEX DISPLAY SIZING

Multi-zone rooms require separate calculations per zone:
- Near zone: viewers 4-12 feet from display
- Middle zone: viewers 12-20 feet
- Far zone: viewers 20-30+ feet

Each zone may have different content requirements:
- Presenters (near) may share spreadsheets (ADM = 4H)
- Audience (far) only needs to see presentations (BDM = 8H)
- Design for the worst case: farthest viewer with most demanding content

MULTI-CIRCUIT LOAD ANALYSIS

For complex systems, aggregate loads by circuit:
1. List every device per circuit with wattage
2. Sum per circuit: must not exceed 80% of circuit capacity
3. Calculate total system thermal load: sum all watts × 3.412 = BTU/hr
4. Verify HVAC capacity covers equipment room thermal load

ACOUSTIC TREATMENT ANALYSIS

Determining if treatment is needed:
1. Calculate room volume (L × W × H)
2. Calculate current absorption (each surface: area × absorption coefficient)
3. Apply Sabine: RT60 = 0.161 × V / A (metric)
4. Compare to target RT60 for room type
5. If RT60 too high: calculate additional absorption needed
   Additional sabins needed: A_new = (0.161 × V / RT60_target) - A_current

workedExamples.given:
Conference room sound reinforcement:
- Loudspeaker to farthest listener (D1): 10m
- Loudspeaker to nearest microphone (D2): 3m
- Talker to nearest microphone (D0): 0.5m
- Talker to farthest listener (DS): 12m
- Number of open mics (NOM): 4
- Feedback stability margin (FSM): 6 dB
workedExamples.asked: Calculate PAG and NAG. Will the system work without feedback?
workedExamples.answer: PAG = -29.16 dB, NAG = 27.6 dB. System will NOT work — must reduce NOM, move speakers closer to listeners, or move microphones closer to talkers. This is a design failure that must be addressed.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using 10×log for distance ratios instead of 20×log — distance/pressure uses 20×log. Also forgetting to subtract FSM.

workedExamples.given:
Training room: 12m × 8m × 3.5m. Surfaces:
- Ceiling (96m²): acoustic tile, α = 0.70
- Floor (96m²): carpet, α = 0.30
- Walls (140m²): painted drywall, α = 0.05
Target RT60: 0.6 seconds
workedExamples.asked: Calculate current RT60 and determine if treatment is needed.
workedExamples.solution:
Volume = 12 × 8 × 3.5 = 336 m³
Total absorption:
- Ceiling: 96 × 0.70 = 67.2 sabins
- Floor: 96 × 0.30 = 28.8 sabins
- Walls: 140 × 0.05 = 7.0 sabins
- Total A = 103.0 sabins

RT60 = 0.161 × 336 / 103 = 54.10 / 103 = 0.525 seconds

Current RT60 (0.525s) < Target (0.6s) ✓
workedExamples.answer: RT60 = 0.53 seconds — within target. No additional treatment needed. The acoustic ceiling tile and carpet provide sufficient absorption.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using room area (96m²) instead of volume (336m³) in the Sabine equation.

lessons.examRelevance: Advanced math combining multiple formulas appears throughout the CTS-D exam. PAG/NAG analysis, DISCAS calculations, and electrical load analysis are the most common multi-step problems. Practice until you can identify which formula to use from the problem description.

knowledgeCheck.question: In PAG calculation, what does a negative result indicate?
options: The system will have echo problems
The system cannot achieve enough gain before feedback
knowledgeCheck.answer: The system cannot achieve enough gain before feedback
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A negative PAG means the system's maximum gain before feedback is less than zero — it will feed back before providing any useful amplification. The design must be modified.

knowledgeCheck.question: A room has a volume of 200m³ and total absorption of 40 sabins. What is the RT60?

memorize: PAG formula with all 6 terms
NAG = 20×log(DS/D0)
Additional sabins = (0.161×V/RT60_target) - A_current
understand: How to interpret PAG < NAG (system won't work)
Why NOM reduction is often the easiest way to improve PAG
practice: Solve at least 5 PAG/NAG problems with different distances and NOM values
Calculate RT60 for rooms with mixed surface materials
examTraps: PAG uses BOTH 20×log (for distances) AND 10×log (for NOM) in the same equation
A negative PAG is a valid result — it means the system design fails
studyNotes.fieldTip: On the exam, set up the entire PAG equation before calculating. It's easy to miss a term if you try to solve it incrementally.

lessons.summary: Advanced CTS-D math requires combining multiple formulas. PAG must exceed NAG for sound reinforcement to work — negative PAG means design failure. Complex display sizing uses the farthest viewer with the most demanding content type. Multi-circuit analysis sums loads per circuit with 80% derating. Sabine equation determines if acoustic treatment is needed by comparing calculated RT60 to target values.

lessons.content:
EXAM REVIEW: DUTIES A & B

These two duties combine for 48% of the CTS-D exam. They test your professional process and coordination skills as much as your technical knowledge.

DUTY A PATTERNS (20%)

Common question types:
1. Stakeholder identification: 'Who should be consulted about [specific requirement]?'
2. Requirement classification: 'Which of these is a functional requirement?'
3. Process sequence: 'What is the FIRST step when beginning a needs assessment?'
4. Site survey: 'What environmental factor is MOST critical for [this room type]?'
5. Program report: 'What should be included in the program report at this stage?'

Key Duty A principles:
- Always start with the client's NEED, not the technology
- Functional requirements describe WHAT, specifications describe HOW
- Site surveys document everything — you can't over-document
- Program reports don't include equipment selections
- The user experience drives design decisions

DUTY B PATTERNS (28%)

Common question types:
1. Trade coordination: 'When should AV requirements be communicated to [the architect/MEP/IT]?'
2. Drawing interpretation: 'What does this symbol on the RCP indicate?'
3. Conflict resolution: 'The HVAC diffuser conflicts with the speaker location. What do you do?'
4. Calculation: 'Calculate the BTU/hr thermal load for this equipment room.'
5. Code compliance: 'Which cable rating is required for this installation?'

Key Duty B principles:
- Early coordination is always better (SD, not CD)
- AV designers don't design electrical or HVAC — they specify requirements for those engineers
- Construction document conventions must be followed exactly
- ADA compliance is non-negotiable
- IT coordination requires understanding networking at a professional level

SCENARIO QUESTION STRATEGY

1. Read the entire scenario before looking at answers
2. Identify the DUTY being tested (A, B, C, or D)
3. Determine the PROJECT PHASE (is this needs assessment, design, construction, or verification?)
4. Look for the key constraint or conflict
5. Eliminate distractors:
   - Actions taken at the wrong phase
   - Technically correct but skipping required steps
   - Actions outside the CTS-D designer's scope
6. Choose the answer that follows proper process AND addresses the specific scenario

scenarios.situation: Practice Scenario 1: A school district wants to upgrade 50 classrooms with interactive displays. The superintendent asks you to recommend a specific display brand and provide pricing.
scenarios.notice: This is a needs assessment scenario. The client is asking for specifications before functional requirements are established.
scenarios.nextStep: Explain that you first need to understand classroom sizes, teaching methods, content types, existing infrastructure, and IT capabilities. Recommend a needs assessment engagement including teacher interviews, classroom surveys, and a technology master plan. THEN you can recommend appropriate technology.
scenarios.whyMatters: The correct CTS-D answer is always 'assess needs before specifying technology.' Any answer that jumps to product recommendations is a trap.

scenarios.situation: Practice Scenario 2: During DD, the IT director says all network traffic must pass through a corporate firewall, but the AV-over-IP system requires multicast traffic between encoders and decoders on a dedicated VLAN.
scenarios.notice: Two valid requirements conflict: IT security policy vs. AV functionality.
scenarios.nextStep: Schedule a coordination meeting with IT to discuss: (1) dedicated AV VLAN that remains behind the firewall but doesn't route through it for local traffic, (2) IGMP snooping configuration, (3) QoS policies that satisfy both AV performance and IT security. Document the agreed solution.
scenarios.whyMatters: CTS-D designers must coordinate, not dictate. The answer that proposes collaboration and documentation beats the answer that bypasses IT requirements or abandons the AV-over-IP design.

lessons.examRelevance: This lesson directly prepares you for the 48% of exam questions covering Duties A and B. The scenario format mirrors actual exam questions. Practice identifying the duty, phase, and best next step.

knowledgeCheck.question: A client asks for a 'state-of-the-art' boardroom. What is the CTS-D designer's FIRST action?
options: Research the latest display technologies and prepare a proposal
Conduct a needs assessment to define functional requirements and constraints
Prepare a budget estimate based on typical boardroom costs
knowledgeCheck.answer: Conduct a needs assessment to define functional requirements and constraints
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The correct first step is ALWAYS needs assessment. 'State-of-the-art' means different things to different clients — you must define what they actually need.

knowledgeCheck.question: During construction, the mechanical engineer changes the HVAC layout, moving a return air diffuser to a location directly above the presenter's position. What should the AV designer do?
options: Ignore it — HVAC is not AV's concern
Accept the change and redesign the microphone system
Issue a formal conflict notice to the project team and propose alternatives that protect audio performance
Contact the HVAC contractor directly to demand they move it back
knowledgeCheck.answer: Issue a formal conflict notice to the project team and propose alternatives that protect audio performance
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The AV designer identifies the conflict (diffuser noise over presenter microphone position), documents it formally, and proposes alternatives through proper project channels. Direct contact with contractors bypasses the process.

Duty B = 28% (coordination with 7 categories of professionals)
Exam time: ~82 seconds per question, 110 scored questions
understand: Why 'assess needs first' is almost always the correct first step
How to eliminate distractors by checking project phase and scope
practice: Practice scenario questions with a timer — 82 seconds per question
For each practice question, identify which duty and task is being tested

Any answer that bypasses proper project channels (going directly to contractors) is wrong
Any answer that skips a required process step is likely wrong, even if technically correct

Duty B requires early coordination (SD phase), proper process (RFIs, not direct contractor contact), and documentation of all decisions. Scenario questions test design judgment — eliminate answers that skip process steps, specify products too early, or bypass proper coordination channels.

lessons.content:
DUTY C EXAM REVIEW (38% — ~42 Questions)

Duty C is the largest domain. Question categories:

1. Conceptual Design (C1 — 11%):
- Display sizing using DISCAS (4H/6H/8H)
- Equipment selection based on requirements
- Signal flow architecture
- Audio system design (speaker coverage, DSP, amplification)
- Video distribution method selection
- Control system architecture

2. Site Adaptation (C2 — 7%):
- Revising designs for actual site conditions
- Resolving conflicts with other trades
- Adapting to architectural changes
- Accommodating existing infrastructure limitations

3. Drawing Production (C3 — 10%):
- Signal flow diagram conventions
- Floor plans, RCPs, elevations
- Rack elevation drawings
- Proper symbols and annotations
- Drawing coordination with other disciplines

4. Documentation (C4 — 10%):
- Equipment schedules and cable schedules
- Bill of Materials
- Specifications (CSI MasterFormat)
- Cable labeling (F501.01)
- Rack design (F502.02)

DUTY D EXAM REVIEW (14% — ~15 Questions)

1. Project Support (D1 — 5%):
- Shop drawing review
- RFI responses
- Change order evaluation
- Site visit observations

2. Performance Verification (D2 — 5%):
- Commissioning procedures (D402.02)
- Audio measurements (SPL, coverage ±3dB, STI)
- Video measurements (brightness, contrast, color 6500K)
- Functional testing

3. Project Closeout (D3 — 4%):
- As-built documentation
- O&M manuals
- End-user training
- Punch list and acceptance
- Warranty handoff

COMPLETE FORMULA QUICK REFERENCE

(Remember: formula sheet is provided on exam)

1. Ohm's Law: V = I × R
2. Power: P = V × I = I²R = V²/R
3. dB (power): 10 × log(P1/P2)
4. dB (voltage/distance): 20 × log(V1/V2 or D1/D2)
5. Inverse square law: -6 dB per doubling of distance
6. Throw ratio: TR = Distance / Width
7. Sabine: RT60 = 0.161 × V / A (metric)
8. BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412
9. Circuit usable load = Rated watts × 0.80
10. 70V amp sizing = Sum of taps × 1.5
11. DISCAS: ADM = 4H, BDM = 8H
12. NOM penalty: -3 dB per doubling
13. PAG = 20log(D1) - 20log(D2) + 20log(D0) - 20log(DS) - 10log(NOM) - FSM
14. NAG = 20log(DS) - 20log(D0)

EXAM DAY STRATEGY

1. First pass (90 minutes): Answer all questions you know immediately. Flag uncertain ones.
2. Second pass (45 minutes): Return to flagged questions. Eliminate obviously wrong answers, then use best judgment.
3. Final 15 minutes: Verify all questions are answered. Check math question answers.

Time management:
- 110 questions in 150 minutes = 82 seconds average
- Don't spend more than 2 minutes on any question — flag and return
- Math questions take longer — budget 3-4 minutes each
- Scenario questions: read the scenario ONCE carefully, then answer

Answer elimination:
- Wrong phase (needs assessment answer during construction phase)
- Wrong scope (structural engineer's decision, not AV designer's)
- Wrong process (skipping required steps)
- Wrong formula (using 10×log for distance, using width for DISCAS)
- Too specific (naming a product brand in a standards question)
- Too vague (general statement when specific action is needed)

CONFIDENCE CHECKLIST

✓ I can identify all four duties and their weightings
✓ I know the difference between functional requirements and specifications
✓ I can read architectural drawings (floor plans, RCPs, elevations)
✓ I can coordinate with MEP, structural, IT, and acoustical professionals
✓ I can calculate display size using DISCAS (4H/6H/8H)
✓ I can design audio systems (70V sizing, DSP signal chain, PAG/NAG)
✓ I can select appropriate video transport technology
✓ I can design control system architectures
✓ I can create signal flow diagrams and equipment schedules
✓ I know all AVIXA standards by number and purpose
✓ I can perform all AV math calculations
✓ I understand the commissioning and closeout process
✓ I can manage my time across 110 questions in 150 minutes

scenarios.situation: Practice: A 40-seat training room needs a display visible from 35 feet away. Content includes detailed CAD drawings. The room has floor-to-ceiling windows on the south wall with no shades.
scenarios.notice: Three constraints: (1) ADM content (4H rule) at 35 feet, (2) high ambient light from uncontrolled windows, (3) 40-seat room.
scenarios.nextStep: Calculate: Minimum image height = 35ft / 4 = 8.75 feet = 105 inches. This exceeds any single flat panel. The uncontrolled ambient light eliminates projection. Solution: Direct-view LED wall with minimum 105" image height, or coordinate with architect to add motorized shading and use projection. Document the options with cost/performance trade-offs.
scenarios.whyMatters: This combines DISCAS calculation, display technology selection, and architectural coordination — a multi-duty question covering A (requirements), B (architect coordination), and C (design selection).

knowledgeCheck.question: An integrator submits shop drawings showing a control processor powered from the same circuit as four amplifiers. The CTS-D designer should:
options: Approve the shop drawing — all devices need power
Return marked 'Revise and Resubmit' — control processor should be on a separate UPS-backed circuit
Contact the electrical engineer to add more circuits
Accept if total wattage is under 80% of circuit capacity
knowledgeCheck.answer: Return marked 'Revise and Resubmit' — control processor should be on a separate UPS-backed circuit
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Control processors should be on clean, UPS-backed power separate from high-current amplifiers. This is a design standards issue the CTS-D designer must enforce during shop drawing review.

knowledgeCheck.question: A conference room signal flow shows: Laptop HDMI → HDBaseT TX → Cat6A (75m) → HDBaseT RX → 86" Display. What is missing?
options: Nothing — this is a complete point-to-point video path
An audio DSP and speakers for the room
knowledgeCheck.answer: Nothing — this is a complete point-to-point video path
knowledgeCheck.explanation: This is a correct point-to-point HDBaseT video path: source → transmitter → Cat6A cable (within 100m limit) → receiver → display. Audio can be embedded in the HDMI signal. Room audio (for conferencing) would be a separate system.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the CTS-D exam time allocation per question?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 150 minutes / 110 scored questions = approximately 82 seconds per question. Budget extra time for math questions and use remaining time for flagged questions.
